div.p: round from the stage doer-keeper, who had told hinfthat I was in the building, I offered to wait, but he said he might be some tiros, so I arranged that he should take back the key. How strangely things fall out. Perhaps if I had only stopped . . There was no general rehearsal on Monday, as old Bagley wanted to keep us as. fresh as possible for the night, but one or two bits of business had to be run through, and some of Us were about the place on and off pretty -well all day. I had had some trouble to get some of the cues for my music to go all right, and Egerton had been pretty: busy; for, as usual, he had been helping Bagley in the stage management, a thing the old man always saw to. There wu a lot of gun-firing in the latter part of the piece, and as rgerton knew a great deal more about such things than anyone else in the theatre, he had undertaken to eivs an eye to this, for the property man was a duffer. °I don't think I had fired a shot since I was a boy in the country. I fancy he and I must have been the last in the theatre,

and we left about the same time to go home to tee. At length the night came. I had bolted back directly after tel., and gone behind. Looking through the cur- tain I could see the house filling fast. Pit and gallery crammed, and every prospect of a good thing. S- was a manufacturing town, and just at that time work was brisk and money plentiful. So at last I slipped into my place in the orchestra, rapped to attention, arid started off on an overture which I had faked up for the occasion out of a set of quadrilles on Irish airs. Some of . _

the lads and lasses in the gallery took these up, and be- gan to sing the choruses. Then the curtain went up, and the play began. Neyer mind about the hilt part of it— how the. wicked squireen VON hold of the title deeds of

the Patriot's estate and eviete him, how the English officer saves the patriot's Meter from the obtrusive atten- tions of the aVhiteboy captain, and how the heroine is lured to the house she thinks is still her lover's, and rescued by his popping out through a doorway known only to himself. Two acts had gone off capitally, each with a call at the end of it, and now the third began. The opening scene—" Outside the Fox Inn at Bally- niakilty," with the arrival of the English troops, dance of peasantry—Bagley had picked up some youngsters in the town who could foot a jig properly, and got them to go on for nothing—and plans laid to secure the patriot, and overheard by Shelah—went off briskly. Then the flats in the front groves shot together, as "The Interior of the Inn," for a comic interlude between the foster brother and the tourist, whilst the carpenters were setting the big scene of "The Gap of Dunloe." I was dalled the Gap. of Dunloe, though Bagley had hesitated for some time over the Leprechaun's Glen, or the Vale of Avoca, but whether it was in the least deg-ree like it I am very doubtful. The fact was that there was a rocky gorge amongst the scenery, that had done duty in a drama of the Indian Mutiny, and after turning the palm tree into pines, and sprinkling shamrocks as big as cheese plates all over the rocks, it did splendidly. The flats parted at length, and revealed it. A. very good scene it was. A rugged gorge with a single pine tree fallen across the summit and forming a bridge. Lights half down. Hurried music, and enter Shelah on her way to warn the patriot that his lurking-place is known, and that the troops arel on the way to it. As she advanced to the footlights to sing her song with her red cloak about her, I thought she had never looked better. My heart seemed to swell in my throat as I gazed at her, and I wonder how I got through the music. There was tremendous applause, and she had to repeat the last verse, and then after a brief soliloquy turned to PIBIIIII6I her hasty journey. More hurried music, and enter the Squireen—Waller Bellamy it was—in hot pursuit. He calls on her to stay, and she refuses. He darts at her, and catches her by the wrist, and they struggle down stage, tum-terrum-tum-terrara. I can recall every note played. She throws him off once, but he catches her again and drags her down a second time. Suddenly she snatches a pistol sticking out from the bosom of his waistcoat, and level's it straight at his head. Chord and attitude. "One step towards me, and you die !" Then she backs slowly up stage to the path leading to the summit of the gorge to a pizzicato accompaniment, turn-tiddy-iddy-tiddy, tuna-tiddy-iddy-tiddy. It was splendidly done as she went slowly up the rocky path, , whilst the Squireen cursed and soliloquised, left centre. More hurried music—martial this time—and arrival of the troops. The Squireen tells the officer, young Heath - cote, to give the order to fire on her. The officer refuses. He is there to combat the rebels to his king, and not to make war on defenceless women. A round of applause. "As a magistrate, I command you, in the king's name, to obey my orders," says the Squireen; " refuse, and you prove yourself a rebel." A howl from the gallery. Despair of the officer. "You ask me, sir, to do an act that would make the cheek of every honest man blush as scarlet ae the coat I have the honour to wear." "1 bid you, sir, stay the progress of a traitor nnd a spy, the bearer of documents on which the lives of hundreds may depend," says the lying Squireen. "Arrali, ma laouchal, blaze away, there's no reason why ye should hit her, surersays the foster-brother, who is acting as guide—a false one, of course—to theesoldiers. Meanwhile, Jessie had been slowly making her way up the rocky path. Ae she reached the summit the moon came heem•behind the clouds, the gas was turned up at the back, and the limelight sent full upon her. How beautiful the girl looked? The hood of her scarlet cloak was thrown back, her fair hair floated about her face like a halo, her dark eyes gleamed out of her pale face, her lipewere compressed, and her features set. It was superb, and there was another burst of applause. She advanced towards the bridge; in another moment she will have crossed it and be in,safety. "Fire, in the king's name fire," cries the Squireen, turning to the soldiers. As she stood:there in her fair young beauty I almost rose in my seat to cry to them to pause. It was so realistic you know. Bang the volley rang out. She was to have darted across the bridge unharmed, though only to fall into the clutch of Egerton,. as the Whiteboy captain, lurking in ambush to intercept her on the other side. Oh, *God ! Instead of bounding across she suddenly stopped and reeled, whilst perhaps only my eye noted a tress of her her hair fly loose like is flash of sunlight. She staggered forward a step, and then fell—fell behind the scene,. and though this. told the audience nothing, the next moment my strained ear caught the sickening thud which told me she had gone sheer down from that giddy height on to the stage. But horror on horror.. Egerton, darting from his. ambush towards her, had scarcely set foot- on the bridge than it gave way, and he ton went down with a tremendous crash. The curtain dropped amidst such a roar of applause as had never. before shaken the walls of the theatre. So realistic a scene had never before been ysitnessed. As it came down something caught in an eddying current of air whirled out from beneath its It was a lock of fair hairs and it flattered down upon my desk. Strange, was it not? But I was no longer there to receive it. I had darted down the orchestra stairs, and hurried at once on to the stage. All was in confusion as I made my way to the back of the scene. Jessie was lying there the centre of a crowd of frightened men and women. Her head, the poor pele face streaked with blood, was on the lap of Miss Cottisfold, who—heaven bless the good-hearted soul !—was sobbing her heart out as she vainly strove to restore Ner to consciousness. Bagley was raving like a madman, and Halford stood looking on like a beirildered'l fool. A little way off another group was clustered' around Egerton, equally motionless. Horriblest mockery of all was the thunder of applause still coming from thern front of the house, the "call" to which their ears were- deaf for ever. To the day-of my death I shall never know what really took place during the next few minutes. I have since- been told that I threw neyselt on my knees beside Jessie.% and went on like a maniac, begging her look up and speak, to me.. They had, they say, quite a job to get me away,. and then a doctor arrived, and she and Egerton were re- moved to two of the dressing-rooms, whilst someone. went before the curtain and dismissed the audience.. I believe I sat in a state of stupor, from which I.was. only aroused aroused by Bagley taking me by the arm, an& say ing something. I seemed to wake up at once, and have all my wits about me,. as I looked him in the eyes. "-Good heavens, Masterton !" he said, he was always partial to me, "what is the meaning of this, my lad'?" "-It is terrible," I gasped out.. •" What a frightfal accident." "Accident. That's just it. There's more than an accident. Try and' pull yourself together. Dies, you' see anything strans,,e.from the front " What do you ?" I asked in arnazerneat. "She was shot!c' " Shot ! " "Yes. The doctor says that she has a couple of bullet S wounds. She may have been dead before slie,fell:7" Bullet wounds I Then the curl must bevel:item shorn from her hes-41,13y a bullet. I was too much, amazed to reply for some-time, and therel managed eo "But the. gunsewho loadedebhem ?" "Egertoneas far as I can make out." "And what does he say ?" I said, for B hardly knew what I wee talking about. "Say! His neck is brasen.7' I do not quite know how. Bagley maneged it, but the doctor was a very old friend: of his, and, at hie, earnest persuasion, I fancy, agreed not to say anything about the bullet wounds at the inquest. Save he. and Miss Cottisfold:who had halved him to disrobe poor Jessie, no one besides Bagley azid myself Isteew of them. The local police were not flyers, and at the, inquest a verdict- of "Accidental Death 'was given in both eases, for lb warethought that Jessie must have eltherbeen startled ley. the noise of the guns or turned dizzy- from the height at which she found herself: The corener,havrever, lectute• d ola Bagley terribly on pandering to a depraved taste foe sensationalism, and the old fellow never got over the business. It pretty well ruined hies, and he died almost a pauper. It was one of those mysteries which will never be , satisfactorily cleared up, though, as / said, in my earn mind I have very little doubt the matter. Bagley's theory was that Egerton, in his mad jealousy, had resolved to slay Jessie, and put bullets in the guns, and had either fallen from an accident, or thrown himself purposely down in an agony of remorse. I thought the former, though old' Page, the chief carpenter, always vowed that the bridge was perfectly safe, and that lie could not account for it giving way as it did. Certainly the only man who had any chance of tampering with the guns was Egerton, and the only pos- sible motive was the revenge of a jealous lover. Yes, I was a discarded lover, too, as yeu say, But not a jealous one, Oh! no.—Cioad-night.

He would read that statement if they wished, but first of ell he would ask the assistant clerk if say communication had been received from the Local Government Board since the last meeting.—The Asstsrarr CLitax said no communication had been received from the Local Government Board on the matter, but there had been by direction of the Guar- dians one sent to the Local Government • Board merely stating that Mr. Mackey had not yet ten- dered his resignation.—Mr. VOISEY then read the following statement, which had been prepared by Messrs. Jeans and Co., on behalf of Mr. Mackey to be sent to the Lose' Government Board, viz: "Mr. Mackey, the master of the Warrington Workhouse has consulted us in reference to the position in which he has been placed in consequence of an alteration which wee made in the date of the account of Mr. John Lledgcoek. It appears from your letter of the 20th July last, which purports to contain an extract from the minute hook of the House Committee, that 'he,' the master, made theulteration, and it seems to us that the decisien of e Local Government Board in requiring Mr. Mackey to sand in his resiguetion is based upon an erroneous impres- sion conveyed by that extract. The minute book shows un- mistakeehly and incontrovertibly that Mr. Mackey did not either make the alteration himself or admit that he had made it, but on the oomerary that it was made by an old man who assisted him in the office. To show you that this was so we send you an exact copy of the entry as it appears in the minute hook as follows :--" The Local Governments Board's letter, dated June 25th, 1886, was read. The Master said, seeing the account had not been rendered by Mr. tiedgcook in time, his clerk, George Webster (' he ' is here inserted in Mr. Jeans' letter in red ink and his clerk, George Webster,' is shown as having been struck through with a pen) made the alteration so as to save as, he thought, any trouble, but the work had been done and the money was due to Mr. Iledgcock " On com- paring this entry with your extract, you will see .that the word "he " has been interpoleted in the copy sent to you where we have inserted it in red ink, the entry as it stood originally being that George Webster made the alteration, the words" his clerk George Webster" having been struck out by the Chairman of the House Committee at the time at the suggestion of Mr. Mackey, who said that the old man Wig dead, he did not wish to put tbe blame upon him.' M. Brown, who entered the minute and struck out the words, will confirm this. Yen will thus see that if the words "his clerk George Webster " be read as part of the original entry, it reads consistently all through without the word "he," and whoever sent you the copy of the entry, must have inserted the word "he " in order as he must be supposed to have thought, to supply what appeared to him to be an omission, and without notic- in how the original entry would be read. This explana- tioreappears to throw quite a different complexion upon the matter, and to remove the ground for the imputation upcn the master that he made the alteration or admitted having done so, he being quite innocent thereof. He appears to have got himself into trouble through his desire not to im putelflame to Webster who was then deadebut that certainly cannot be sufficient ground' for bringing down upon himself such a tremendous punishment as deprivation of office after having spent upwards of 25 years and devoted the best part of his life in the service of the Warrington and other unions. We have ourselves seen the minute book containing the above entry, and which is of course open to yonainspection as well, and it is clear that there has been no tampering with the entry and that it originally stood as it now stands exactly according to the extract above given, without the word " he." We trest that under the circum- stances the Board will reconsider the matt3r and not inflict upon Mr. Mackey such a severe punishment as deprivation of office after so many years' faithful service. •We may state that a large number of the Guardians see hew toe mis- take originated, and are entirely opposed to the dismissal of Mr. Mackey, and also that a large number of the outside public feel that Mr. Mackey is being harshly and unjustly dealt with."—Mr. RATCMIFFE thought it ought to have been notified to every guardian that that matter was to be re- opened that day.—The CHAIRMAN said that was his opinion too, but he thought it best that Mr. Vaisey should rnakeehe statement he had made. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

PEAS.--It was fbrmerly the aim of Pea growers to have - the first growing on the 4th of June. the birth-day of George the Third,. and those situated in unfavourable localities resorted to all kinds of expedients to secure their object. All known protective measures were brought into use, even to sowing under glass and trans- planting afterwards into the open ground. In our days, with improved early varieties, it requires no great skill to produce Peas even earlier than thht in most gardens south of the Trent, but as yet we have not heard of any being picked on the 4th of June, in the north, without glass protection, close upon the time of gathering. Sowing ie autumn was a favourite practice, and is still with some growers, but it rarely proves in advance of those sown in January, or as soon in the year as the weather permits, and the yield is always inferior, in con- sequence of the numerous enemies the seeds and plants have to encounter, for no sooner do the seeds begin to swell than rats and mice commence their tunnelling operations, along the whole of the rows in search of the seed, and should any escape their notice and become plants, scarcely are they above ground before the slugs and sparrows attack them. Of course spring-sown Peas are in a Measure similarly exposed, but with ordinary attention the rows are never so gappy: The seeds .are not so long in the ground before germinating, and are . above ground without being discovered by rats and mice. If the birds can only be kept sway for a fortnight or so the seeds will be too far advanced for them to interfere with them, and the increased supply of food in other chatinelS will attract the birds' attention. Slugs can be kept under by sprinkling scot and limb along the side of the rows early in tee morning in mild weather, at the salve time dashing it between the plants at the base. Those who wish to test the autumn sowing plan should sow at once in drills 61n. deep and three to four feet asunder, and sow much thicker than in spring, in order to allow for seeds of weak germinating powers and other • contingencies. A south border should be selected for the - purpose, and the rows should run north and south. Vacant spaces—ground that has been cleared of late croPs of peas, French beans, and scarlet runners—shoukl be either forked, dug, or ridged, in order to expose it to the influence of frost and other agencies. The latter is a favourite occupation with many practitioners, and if the hasesof the ridges are made about two feet distant. they are • convenient for planting potatoes in, and the manure can be put either underneath the sets or on the top, according to the planter's fancy. Where the ridges, are levelled they afford ample covering for the tubers. Ridging ground is perhaps one of the best methods of dealing: with ground which has to lie fallow ever the winter, as so much more surface is laid exposed to the elements than by any other practice; and, moreover, the land lying high in the ridge is so much drier than that lying fiat that it can be worked several weeks sooner in some seasons—a great advantage in the spring of the• year.

_ _ THH FHONT GARDEN.—BIIibS : Few things- are more charming in the front garden than patches-of spring, flowering bulbs, and their popularity has increased ofF late years, The displays made in our public, parks and; gardens have no doubt stimulated many to take up. their. culture who did not think of attempting, it before. The increased demand seems to have augmented the. sUpply„and prices have been brought so low as to be. withinthe means of the .humble cottager. Those who. deal in. them are now often. prepared to sell their surplus, stocks at prices much below those in their catalogues rather-than that they should spoil. Few gardeners would_ Purchase Snowdrops after this date, their stock having. been,sscured and plant.F.d some time back, and the,dif- ference. between them and those planted, now would be that the latter would be weaker for a year or two: They are best planted in patches of not les.s than a dozen bulbs- about 2in. distant and about 41n. deep.. The natural soil should 'betaken out one fost deep anda, por- tion. of it mixed with decayed manure, .leaf mould and sand or road grit. Da.the centre of each patch. of these and all other bulbs ,insert a piece of wire 81n. deep and , of the thickness of an ordinary lead pencil with a total length of 1A- inches,. so that the portion abeve. ground, will always indicate the whereabouts of the. bulbs. Otherwise serious mischief may accrue when. the beds are dug for other plants. Tulips are another eass of bulbs that should be planted at once, if at all; the ortho- dox season being September and October. Plant, a uni- form depth of six: inches, and if the bulbs- are covered with sand it will help to preserve, them 2tom decaying. No less than Sve should be in a clump, one in the centre and the others six inches distant around it. Crocus look well in a, row near the pat Lik the above, their planting should not be further delayed, and the remarks I as to planting we equally applicable to them. I THE WHlDOTT.—Echeyeria Retusa is a plant little known, even to gardeners. Upon our recommendation,, a cottager. undertook to grow it in his window, and though the apartment is lighted with gas, the thick% fleshy leaves of the Echeveria is not affected, and, is flowering as freely as if in a greenhouse. Like most succUtants, it requires but little water during the winter and early spring tnonths, and it should not be applied unless the soil feels dust dry on the top. Pot as soon as growth commences, in loam, and one-fourth leaf mould, with, a sprinkling of coarse sand, to which may be added a few- small nodules of old- mortar, broken crocks front flower pots (but not household ware), also broken bricks, and none of the pieces should be larger than a filbert or Iless than a pea.

TO BABY CATCHING SUNBEANS. 7 Thou pretty little laughing elf, )-r Thou replication, of myself, _ How much thou lov'st the merry sport Of catching sunbeans, which, when caught, Yield nothing to tilt) tiny grasp, Yet light the hand that cloth them clasp.

Thy sport's an emblem of the ways • Of children of far older station, WI, Who vainly strive to catch the rays That pierce the soul's dim habitation. They eager seek God's truth to seize, In all its myriad forms of beauty ; But it eludes their outstretched grasp, Kir* 'Yet lights them on the path of duty. rso.t", But just as when I ope this door , Upon you breaks a flood of light, - And all the beams thou saw'st before Co-mingle in the radiance bright— So when the angel Death shall come, And ope the door that separates Our mortal life and heavenly home, - And usher us to brighter states-- The little rays of truth that here • Perplec us as we strive to see From their faint gleam.a meaning clear . Of life and dark futurity, Shall mingling meet our raptur'd sight, Wherepod the Sun cloth ever shine; , Where we shall live in true delight Illumined with His rays divine. H. ROSE.

THE YISCOSITT OF Mmx.—The Country Gentleman BY THE CUTICURA REMEDIES., makes a preliminary report of some experiments which have been going on for some time in the New York station in regard to the " viscous " or sticky property BY THE CUTICURA REMEDIES. in milk. That is, an effort has been made to show the different degrees of viscosity in two fluids by a scale BY THE CUTICURA REMEDIES. register, so that comparison can be made in figures to 3 show how much fluids vary in this respect from each ' other and from water, say, in which the particles move and separate readily, and with little tendency to adhere or become "ropy." One result reached is a probability that a new test of some value has been found for dis- tinguishing genuine butter from adulterations with other fats. Pure butter liquefied with potash was found to be much less viscous than any adulterated butter. The most sticky sample of genuine butter registered a much lower degree of viscosity than the least sticky of the adulterations. A very minute proportion of neutral oil added to pure butter Increased the degree of viscosity at once and appreciably. Of more immediate practical interest to dairymen Is the study of this quality in milk. The first study seems to show that undue vis- cosity in butter is a sign of adulteration or counterfeit. The second seems to show that this quality of sticki- ness or tenacity between the particles of milk is bad for butter-making, and that the leas glutinous the milk the better it is for butter. SILAGE TOR FATTENING CAT/I:E.—A great blow to silage as food for fattening cattle is given by Dr. Voelcker's report in the Royal Agricultural Society's Journal on the feeding experiments carried out by the Royal Agricultural Society at Woburn in 1884-85 and 1885-86. In every instance in which grass or clover silage was pitted against swedes or mangels, the gain in live weight was considerably in favour of the roots. This was the case whether the silage was sweet or sour, though it is only fair to point out that but one experi- ment was made with the sweet variety, and that on only two bullocks. The quantities of roots and hay and silage respectively given were regulated as closely as possible in proportion to the relative percentages of dry matter, woody fibre, and nitrop;en, and the same quanti- ties of cake and maize meal were served out to both lots of animals in each of the experiments. In 1884-85 the animals fed on swedes and hay-chaff showed an average daily gain per head in lire weight of 2,11 b., while those which had silage gained only 141 b. per day. When mangels were given instead of swedes, the result was still more in favour of the roots, the daily gain for sixty days being 21b. each for the root-fed (swedes first and mangels afterwards) bullocks, and 11-121 b. for those which had silage. After that the experiment was re- versed, the animals which had been fed on roots getting silage, and vies 'sorsa. In this experiment mange's and clover hay -were tried against clover silage, and the daily gain was 2 1-51 b, to the credit of the former and only *lb. to that of the latter. In the following year the silage was' made from a superior quality of grass to that used before, and the results were an average daily gain of 21b. soz. per head during 113 days in the bullocks fed on roots and hay-chaff, and 21b. loz, in those fed on sour silage. Two bullocks, fed for 54 days on roots and hay- chaff, gained 11b. Inca. daily per head, and two receiv- ing sweet silage 11b. lox. Oat silage. on the other hand, produced a daily gain of 21b., against lilb. for roots and straw-chaff; and in a second trial with the same foods the figures in the same order 2 3-71 b. and 1 3-71 b. BREEDING GoOD Sows.—lt is not strange that we hear the complaint that the sows of improved breeds are not so prolific, or do not suckle as well as do the mongrels. These latter have not been full fed so as to develop the habit of laying on flesh and fat until that habit has be- come so strong as to enfeeble the natural one of animals in a state of nature. Select the sows of the herd which have the most desirable form and characteristics, and mate them with boars which are the best types of the breed, and then from their produce select the best sow pigs for your brood sows. Now, let such sow pigs be separated from the pigs intended for market, and given all the range the farm will allow. Exercise is essential for the hardening of muscle and bone, and for securing the highest development of lung and digestive power. With such range, of course the young sows should get that variety of feed which shall meet the demands of an omnivorous feeder, and especially a herbivorous animal. Together with the grass and roots and herbs of great variety these young brood sows will feed upon must be supplied a few beans or peas, and the like, as to give supplies for highest development of bone and tissue. Liberality in feed, both as to quality and variety, as well as quantity, will, under such management, give us such a a lot of brood sows as can by no possible means be produced from the confined method of one article of diet in a limited rans,re or close pen. The young sow or boar intended for breed- ing must be fed and handled so as to produce bone, tissue, and vigour. rather than flesh and fat. To secure the latter we resort to abundance of rich feed, with the repose that comes with a full supply of the animal wants. To secure the vitality vigour which will impress itself upon posterity, the sire and dam must have the active life, the outdoor exercise, and muscle-building feed which give endurance and force. Here we have the general principles which mark the difference between the uses to which we expect the two classes of hogs to be put. There is a wide differ- ence in these, and let the character of the feed and management agree with the uses intended, and we shall soon hear less of the degenderating tendency of im- proved stock, and learn niece of the improvements pos- sible, when the means are suited to the end.

Straight as a die, too, brought up in the profession from her childhood. Well up in herbusiness, only caring about it, and having no friends, no interests, and no am- bition beyond the theatre. The breed has died out, lam afraid. Ladies and all kinds of' outsiders flock into the profession nowadays, and think about fifty outside matters, from lawn tennis upward, instead of the one sole thing, the shop. They gush a great deal as to their art, but that is:about all they can do. In my early days they would have had to keep hard at work learning fresh parts, which would have been ever so much better for them. Why, I can run over whole families of theatre folk living amongst themselves, and having no more knowledge of any other life than their own than of the laws of etiquette in China. Society! Actors and actresses did not know the meaning of the word. I remember a very big man from the provinces coming to play leading parts at Drury Lane who had never entered a drawing-room in • his life. His whole idea of existence beyond the theatre was confined to country lodgings and hotel .smoking-rooms. But he could play Shakespeare. There, there, I am doddering on as only a fogey and a failure can dodder. Well, Jessie Denton was, as I said, one of our company—singing chambermaid, but with a chance of developing into something better by hard work. I She was a pretty girl, a very pretty girl, and so bright, so brisk, and so good-humoured that no one could help 'loving her. Yes, I loved her myself as I have never loved any other woman. We had both been in the com- pany some time, and spent much of it together. I did all I could to help her on with her singing and music, and many an hour we passed together at the piano when- ever we were fortunate enough to come across such an instrument. They were not so plentiful in theatrical lodgings as you find them now I sometimes had it on my tongue to tell her what I felt for her, but always checked myself. I am an observant man, as I said be- fore, and I saw that although she liked me as a friend there was, as yet, but little chance of anything more. So I waited and hoped for a change—and let the chance slip for ever. We had lost several old stagers about that time, and amongst the new blood replacing them was our leading man, Percy Halford, a. young nincompoop Who, on the strength of a good face, an imposing figure, and a full voice, thought himself fit to play anything from Romeo downwards. A regular duffer I always thought him, but he went down, even in the provinces, where, I maintain, audiences have a far better appreciation of real acting than in London. Women who really ought to have known better used to make eyes at- him from the boxes, and languisle in admiration till he grew to think himself no end of a genins. Some idiots, too; used to write him admiring letters,and barmaids and such-like would make up to him most shamefully. Ido not say that he was a bad fellow, but he was an insufferable lump of conceited egotism; and he was actually as much in love with any- one besides himself as he could be with Jessie Denton. Much to the disgust of Miss Cottisfold, our leading lady, a fine figure of a woman still, and one greatly admired. Yet more so to that of Richard Egerton: Egerton was a clever fellow and something of a mystery. Like Haitord, he was a new-comer amongst us. What his real mune was—for Egerton was plainly an assumed one—l do not know. From one or two facts it was evident that he had been at some time or other at sea, and I fancy that he had got into some scrape and been forced to leave the Royal Navy. 'Very likely I should say, for he had a vile temper, to my mind. oh, he was a pleasant companion enough, but' as peppery as I Lucifer, and when once roused I should say capable of ! anything. Two or three times I have known him to get ! into.a row, and to fight like a demon. Once he went so far as to strike me, though I must say he apologised afterwards, and we soon made it up. Not much of an lactor, but still a fairly clever one considering his lack of early training, and good at villain's parts, .for which, his dark face and lissom figure fitted him. But he had one great pull over the rest of us, in that he had evidently 'seen a great deal of the world, and could put us right on ,! all manner of points. Then he was quick and handy, as a sailor always is, and would devise all manner of tricks I and dodges for overcoming difficulties as to scenery and I the like, which made hima great favourite with old Bee!- ! ley, though those two used to quarrel, too, at times. An ! nothing would satisfy him but to fall in love with Jessie I Denton. I We were at S— at the time for the. Easter season. 1 Bagley had resolved to put up an original drama for I Easter Monday, and not a had one. It was .shortly after I the production of the "Colleen Bawn," and as there was a run- on Irish pieces, and a large Irish population in the town to. boot, lie set the company at work on a play lie christened "Mayourneen Asthore ; or the Green Glades of Glendalough." I do not in the least know what this title meant, nor indeed its relation to the play itself; but then, as Mr. Hollingshead once pointed out in con- nection with a kindred advertisement, it looked well on the bills and pleased the public. 'lt was like all Irish dramas, though as originally translated the scene was laid in Brittany during the struggle between the Royal- ists and Republicans. There was a young patriot and his sweetheart, and a wicked squireen who was his rival, and an English officer in love with the patriot's sister, and a desperado captain of Whiteboys in bye with her too, and a foxy agent, and a faithful foster-brother, with a comic tourist for him to play up at. But the real heroine of the piece was played by Jessie Denton. She was a youg peasant girl named Shelah—r have noticed that all peasant girls in dramas are named Shelah when they are not called Oonagh or Norah—cherishing a hope- less love for the patriot, and going through fire and water to serve him; arrying messagesond foiling plots, and Ido not know what else. A very good part it was, and a better one in some respects than she had ever had a chance of playing. Indeed, Miss Cottisiold was some- what jealous, and expressed an opinion, that she ought to have had it herself. But as she was—well, imposine in presence, she reflected that it was hardly her line to go scrambling about precipices, and escaping from ruined manors, so she badgered Bagley into having her own part written up. He wedged in a fine moonlight solilioquy, a in Juliet, on a balcony—there is always a lot of moonlight in Irish pieces—for her to deliver in the fourth act; and, as her arms were still very good and her elocution her strong point, she was satisfied. Every- one else, for a wonder, was content with his or her part, and we worked away splendidly, whilst old Bagley chuckled at the prospect of a big success. Just about this time the climax came. Jessie showed herself wonderfully clever as Shelah,. and there was no doubt of her marring the hit of the piece. I wonder' whether the thought entered Percy- Flalford's mind that a girl capable of such things would- make a .capital with! from a professional point of view. At any rate, he spoke to her, and got an answer. So did Dick Egerton, and, so did I. Not the same one though. Perhaps if I had spoken earlier—but there, I will not say any mane; I cannot bear to -think of it. I met Egerton the very ater- noon on which I had asked Jessie to be my wife,. He seemed wild and excited, and I fancy he had been drinking.. He caught me by the arm. "What, you too, Teddy, oldman ?" he said, andlooked me in the race and laughed. "The barber's block has got the best of both of us this time." I understood him, I though how lie knew of it I could not tell. Then he I would insist on my turning into a bar with hire. I fancy as he drank up his liquor he muttered something like "curse the jilt," but / will not be certain.. He was, though, very strange that afternoon; and, knowing his teenper, I had an idea that he would go and pick a quarrel with Halford, and indeed, hinted as much in order to check him; but he did not., and was all right at the theatre that night. Still, two or three times during the-next day or so his manner was very strange, and I spoke to one or two people about it. At the time, they said they did not 'notice it, but afterwards, when I reminded them of it, they said they recollected it perfectly. Easter Monday was the night for the production of the new piece, and on Easter Sunday I had to go round to the theatre to look after some music I had forgotten to bring away the night before. I got the key from the stage door-keeper, who lived close by, and went in. I was some time in finding what I wanted, and, just as I got to the door, heard a knock at it. It was Egerton. He said that he wanted COMO things, and had come

THE BULGARIAN SITUArION. TURKEY AND PRINCE MiNGRELIA. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAL—A circular note which the Porte despatched to the Powers me the 4th inst. states that since the recent events in Bulgaria the situation in the Prin- cipality has been abnormal, and that so long as it continues no one can say what the future will be—a condition of affairs which dieeetly affects the interests of the Imperial Government. The circular proceeds to state that the Bul- garian Government, desiring a settlement to terminate this state of things, addressed its Suzerain, as the sole real and legitimate Power, requesting the latter te designate a can- didate for the Bulgarian throne, Russia having proposed the Prince of Mingrelia, and the Porte haying no objection to offer, the circular calls the attention of the Powers to the matter, inviting their co-operation te effect a speedy I settlement. THE OPERATIONS IN BURMATI—EXPEDITION TO Tim SHAM STATES. British operations in Burmah are taking a wider scope than anyone.suppoeed was intended when General Preader- gest made his triumphal entry into Mandalay. MANDALAY, SATIIIIDAL—EarIy in January an expedition will start for the Shan States, probably consisting of 350 British troops and 750 Ghoorkae, with a company of sap- pers, four mountain and twe Gardner guns, on mules. The route will be through the Mattik Pass, 50 miles south-east of Mate,alay. The object is to establish a post to guard the eastern flank of the railway. SEVERE FIGHTING IN BURMAH. RANGOON, MONDA.Y.—On Friday, twenty despite Bur- ' prised a stockaded thane at Mahabourg, nearlee padan, held by six Bengaleee and seven Burmese police. Four Benga- lees were kilted and one severely wounded. None of the Burmese were injared. The thane was burned, end arms and ammunition were 1111rried off by the daeoits. MA'NDALAY, TIIIIEIDAL—CoIOnei. Carey, of the Royal Artillery, has been thrown from his horse, and has sus- tained a fracture of the skull. His recovery is sensidered doubtful. Lieutenant Teesdale has attacked a cargo stockade at Pyanhlai, aid dislodged the rebels, killing thirty of their number. The column at Nyngyan, under the command of Colenel Holt, has attacked the rebel leader, Sanpai, who occupied a strongly entrenched position. The brother of Sanpai and a number of his follewere were killed. FRANCE —THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS. M. de Freycinet announced on Saturday in the French Chamber of Deputies that as the Ministers had resigned , they could not take part in the debate on the Budget, and he demanded the adjourament of the Chamber. A proposal' that the sittiag should be suspended was rejected, and the House adjourned. FORMATION OF A NEW FRENCH CABINET. PARIS, WEDNESDAY, 7 PalL—At a later interview with M. Greyy this afternoon, M. Goblet yielded to the pressing request of the President, and accepted the task of forming a new Cabinet. PARIS, THURSDAY.—It is now expected that the greater part of the late Ministry will remain in the new Cabinet be- ing formed by M. Goblet, and that the new Ministers will only be nominated for the departments of Finance, Foreign Affairs, Interior, and Justice. M. Dauphin is stated to have accepted the porfolio of Finance. GERMANY.—THE NEW ARMY BILL. _ Count Von Moltke addressed the German Reichstag, on Saturday, on the new Military Bill. He stated that an al- liance with France, which might well be ealculated to as- sure the peace of Europe, was impossible so long as public opinion in that country demanded the surrender of two pro- vinces which Germany was strongly determined never to ' give up. The allianave with Austria was valuable but a great state must rely upon its own strength. The bill, said the count, bad been compiled not only with a view to what W&5 most necessary from a military poiat of view, but also with due regard to what was financially attainable, though where such weighty questions as the military strength and defence of the country were involved financial eonsiderae tions mast be set aside. The whole world knew that thee' did not contemplate conquest. but it might also learn that they intended to keep what they had, and were resolute and armed to this end. The War Minister intimated that he would only be prepared to give detailed explanations of the bill in committee if he could reckon upon his statemeats being treated as aonidential. The Minister added that the increase of the army would not only result in preventing Germany hemming involved in war, but would also prove that she could show a proper vigour in other quarters with a view to the maintenance of peace. Upon the close of the debate the bill was referred to a committee. AMERICA.—THE PRESIDENTIAL MESSAGE.-- FENIANISM. WASHINGTON, MONDAY,—Prosideat Cleveland's message communicated to Congress to-day says, concerning fisheries' question, that negotiations have been instituted to obtain an agreement with Great Britain for promulgation of such a joint interpretation mad definition of the articles of the convention el 1818, as should secure Canadiau rights from encroachment by United States fishermen, and ensure the enjoyment by the latter of the priyilegesAke convention guaranteed, and it was hoped an acceptable conclusion would soon be reached. It is recommended that a small naval vessel be presented to Liberia for protecting the revenue on the coast, and announced that, negotiations will be initiated with _lexica° for a new and enlarged treaty of commerce and navigation. The message recommends that the President be authorised to discharge persons committed for extradition, where he may consider their surrender im- proper, and favours an international •opyright arrangement and abolition ot foreign works of art. The income is stated to be more than aver in excess of the public necessi- ties. All the debt now payable will be paid, if. present rate prevails, within a year. The President recommends that with due regard to the present condition of revenue the laws might be amended so as to cheapen the necessaries of life, and give freer entrance to raw materials. He again urges the suspension of compulsory silver coin- age, and concludes by vigorously defending civil service reform. ' PHILADELPHIA., MONDAY—The " Record " to-day pub- lishes a report stating that O'Donovan Roses has been chosen as chief of the allied Felnians of Philadelphia, and that their programme includes secret intrigues in Canada, with a view to creating discontent with England, and the despatch of emissaries to Australia with the same object. 'THE SUEZ CANAL. CAIRO, THIIRSDAY.—In regard to the negotiations pend- ing between Englaad and France relative to the Suez Canal, it is understood England declines to entertain the French proposal for the neutralisation of the Canal, if it is intended thereby to bar the passage of her fleets in time of war. COLLISION OFF THE COAST OF QUEENS- LAND. MELBOURNE, THITR.SDA.L—A. collision has occurred off the coast of Queensland between the steamers Kellawara and Helen Nicholl. The Keilawara sank. Forty-two per- sons were drowned, including the centain of the KeiLawara and six of the crew of the Helen Nicholl. The latter vessel sustained great damage.

CONFERENC E OF LIBERAL UNIONISTS. A. largely attended Conference of Liberal Unionists Was held on Tuesday in Willis's Rooms, London. The Marquis of Hartington presided, and read a letter from Mr. Bright, who said he had no hope of a more moderate policy from Mr. Gladstone, whose allies in Ireland were driving matters to an extremity. l‘tr. Chamberlain telegraphed that if the discarded Scheme were abandoned the Unionist Liberals would be ready to discuss with the Separatists any safe scheme, but that abandonment was indispensable. Lord HARTINGTON, in addressing tbe meeting, regretted that more Liberals did not join them, and admitted that the cause Of the union was only succegsfully defended by an alliance with the Conservative party. Their own course of action must depend on that taken by the Government, the Liberal OPoosition, and the Irish party, and upon the state of affairs in Ireland itself. As to the chances of reunion, the speeches of the Opposition leaders laid down as a necessary basis of t the concession .of an Irish Parliament and future —a concession to which the Unionists could not agree, holding it to be incompatible with the real union of the Empire Empire and the real supremacy of the Imperial Parlia- ment. The Government had declared that they would not be resPonsible for any measure giving Home Rule to Ire- land in any form, and of that declaration he and his friends approved, So far, be thought, even the most hardened Redical had had no cause to complain of what the Govern- ment Was doing in the matter of Irish administration. In other matters the Government had made great promises, and he could not but think that the union of the Conserva- tives with a suction of the Liberal party would have an in- fluence on the whole course of Conservative policy, and enable them seriously 0 undertake some of those neoaesary reforms, the adoption of which they knew to be the only condition on which the lasting alliance of the Unionist Liberals could possibly be secured. He thought ne settlement of the Irish ques:ion would be reached without a final conflict between the forces of order and disorder. Such an agitation as was going on was in 7, and any Gov m ernent must, reeiat it by every sairinaliebtsPower. Upon Mr. Gladstone awl his Heaton- itautal nf rested a grave responsibility. Mr. Gladstme could p t ora eak he which would dissolve the alliance between the Liberal party and the Irish Nationalists until the agi- tation Wag abandoned and suppressed, and if that word were delayed the credit of the Liberal party would be seri- ously endangered. Lord &aortae moved a resolution de- claring it to be the duty of Liberal Unionists not to relax their efforts, in view of the agitation by which the union between Great Britain and Ireland was still menaced. His Lordship said the Dissentient Liberals took uot)on themselves a great responsibility when they separated from their former colleagues, and they would ' not now he easily diverted from the coarse they had adop- ted. ,Tho resolution was seconded by Mr. George Dixon, M.P., who, sPc''l'ing as a Radical Unionist, said he would do nothing to bring back a majority pledged to carry out the policy of the Home Rulers. Sir T. E. Colebrooko, Mr. T. W. Russell) NIT., and Mrs. Fawcett supported the reso- lution, which was carried unanimously. Another re,olu- don, in favour of the establishment and support of Liberal Unionist Associations or committees in the different consti- tuencies, was, on the motion of Mr. Herteage,M.P.;senonded by the Duke of Westmilleter, adopted; and the Conference separated. In the evening a banquet was held at the Hotel Metro- peleo aad was largely attended by peers, members of the

He evoked loud cheering by pointing out that the Unionist leader though not in (anti WWI Yirtuik i 1 y in power. He commented on the overtures for reunion which had been made, and said the Unionists were askacl to "join Glad- stone, Parnell, Labouchere, and Dillon." • .` LIBERALISM IN CHESHIRE. Under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation the Liberals of Cheshire and the border towns of Lancashire, but more particularly the members of the party who reside within the area of the Nortlp,vich Parliamentary Division, had an op- portunity on Monday of affirming their allegiance to the principles of progress and reform. Repre- sentatives from all the divisions of Cheshire, and from Liverpool, Warrington, Widnes, St. Helens, and Newton assembled at Runcorn on the afterncion of that day to take part in a conference, in which they were aided by several well-known members of Parliament, and the chief officers of the Federation. The proceedings, which occupied upwards of two hours, were characterised by an earnestness and thoroughness that augeirs well for the success of the party in this part of the country, notwithstanding the recent reverses they have eustained. The in- fluence of Mr. Gladstone'e name was at potent and inspiring as of yore, and the mention of it called forth the' most enthusiastic demonstrations. Ire- land, of course, occupied the chid considera- tion in the assembly, and the manner in which the observations of the various speakers were received showed that instead of retiring from the position taken up by their great leader, the party were more resolved than ever to carry on their previously declared determination to deal justly and righteously with the sister isle. Judging by the applause by which reference to these sub- jects was received, the reform of the land laws and of the licensing system were held next in im- portance to Ireland, although no definite proposi- tions were made in regard thereto. Altogether, the feelings of the Conference were of the most Radi- cal tendency. In the evening a publie meeting was held in the Public Hall, and was admirably con- ducted by Mr. R. Shaw. In consequence of about 400 seats being reserved at a low fee, the uncom- foitable rushing and crushing that is the usual ac- companiment of political gatherings was altogether avoided, and although the building was not so crowded as many Liberal gatherings previously have been, the hall was well filled. The Marquis of Ripon, who was the guest of the chairman, was the central figure in the evening's proceedings, and de- livered a carefully reasoned and eloquent speech on the Irish difficulty of an hour's duration. (Hear, hear.) The recent developments in Ireland must be a mai- ter of regret to them all. They were grievously sorry for • this perpetual recurrence of agitation, on the one side run- ning into ontrage,and coercive legislation on the other. It was a sondition of things we in England could not under- stand, because we could not enter into and comprehend the Irishntaaht relation to the law. When a man cre- ated property as the Irish tenant had created it, and found the law always backing his landlord in exacting more and 1 more in proportion to his success and labour, his natural I sense of justiee revolted. Sir M. Hieks•Beach said recently he believed the fact was that to too many Irishmen the law I had seemed a foe, because they had no confidence in the ; justice of ite administration. He believed that if it were possible to wipe away tie effect of the introduction of the Home Rule Bill, both on the official mind and the people at large, to infuse fresh vigour and firmness in the administra- tion, that the rights of the poor man, as well as of the rich would be respected, and that the law should never be used as an instrument of oppression—he believed that if these leseons could he taught to the Irish people the victory would be won. The Liberals believed that too--(hear,hear) —but he did not say that the method of doing this was by straining the law as it stood. The Liberals held that there was a better and a nobler method which their great leader had taught them in the present year. (Cheers.) There was never a more baseless superstition than this reverence for a union which was never accepted, but bad been consistently and constantly opposed by one of the two parties to it. Yet, for the sake of keeping the form, and not the real essence, of a out m between two peoples, there were people even who called them- selves Liberals who would support a Tory Go- vernment in trying to keep on the miserable eye ton of the past. First, it was "a steady course of honest government with as little of legislation as possible," then it was local government in some form such as England wan's, and then it was "fresh vigour and firm- ness in the Administration."
