Tee CHAIIZMAN, who was received with applause, said that so recently had he expressed his views upon the Irish question that he should not attempt to say anything Upon that matter, especially as they had distinguished speakers present, whom, he was sure, they were all most willing to hear. He woald, therefore, not occupy their time, or keep them from the treat which he was sure they would have. He then called upon the Marquis of Ripon to address the meeting. The Marquis of 'lnsane, who was on rising to speak re- peatedly cheered, said that before proceeding to observations upen any other topic he must offer his hearty congratula- tions upon the activity that was being shown in every part of the country—and especially under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation—by the Liberal party at the present time. (Cheers.) It was not long ago since they were told upon high Ministerial authority that they (the Liberal party) were "sick unto death." (Laughter, and a "It doesn't look like it.") He quite agreed with that remark; it did not look like it. (Cheers.) So convinced had their opponents become that their diagnosis of the dis- ease of the Liberals was an erroneous one that they were holding up the energy and activity of the Liberals as ex- amples which should be followed by their own friends— (cheers)--end were somewhat complaining of the back- wardness of some of their supporters as compared with the Neal and energy that animated the Liberal party. That energy appeared to him to be full oflproinise for the future. (Cheers.) Defeats, no doubt, were disagreeable things, but they might very easily be turned to good acceunt. If they made proper use of their defeats they might build up upon the foundations of those misfortunes the solid foundation of future success—(cheers)—and he trusted such would be the case in that as in ether parts of the country. What Liberals must do was to organise themselves thoroughly, throughout the country, to bring themselves into close com- munication with'every part ofehe various constituencies, and to do their utmost by discussion in each locality, and by intercourse with the new voters in every district, to sweep away misrepresentations and to refute fallacies. (Cheers.) , Now, when they were not engaged in conflict, when they were resting from the actual conlict of an election, was the time in which they might set to work to remove from the minds of the pecple the erroneous impressions which argu- ments used clueing the heat of an election might have pro- duced. The Liberal party at the present time had to en- counter two perfectly distinct kinds of difficulties. In the first piece they had to encounter undoubtedly an increase in the Tory party, and also they had to encounter a series of difficulties within their own ranks upon a question of very great importance, and what was a vital question at the last general election. Now, in respect to the first of these diffi- culties they might be at ease, and trust to the effect upon the country of the few Years or of the few months of Tory Government. (Cheers.) They knew what was the effect of the few years of Tory Government on their accession to power in 1874, and how thoroughly sick the country had become of them and of their policy at the time of the great general election of 1880. 'BO it would be again. Let them alone, and in a very short time the Liberals would have re- gained the whole of the ground lost by any increase of Tory power at the time of the general election. He hoped that the meeting of Liberal Unionists to be held next day would tell the public frankly what course they intended to pursue. They might ask of them, with all respect, what was they course they intended to pursue with regard to these questions, apart from Irish questions, In which the Liberal party feels a deep interest at the present time. (Cheers ) What were their views and intentions with res- pect to the great questions of land law reform ; local self-government, the reform and improvement of laws of registration and election; and which was the course which they were likely to pursue with respect to certain questions which are being pressed prominently forward in the neighbouring principality of Wales? (Cheers.) They had a right to ask if the Liberal Unionists, although they differed from the majority of the party on the Irish ques- tion, still adhered to those broad principles which the party bad always hitherto possessed. Were they going to sup- port In Parliament now, as they had most of them hitherto supported, the great principles of the Liberal creed; or was Liberalism for the fetter° to consist in sitting upon one side of the house and voting on the other? (Cheers.) He did not believe there were many men amongst them who would consent to adopt the latter course. The majority of them, at all events, were prepared to adhere to the pleO.ges of their lives to Liberal principles. They knew that the Liberal Unionists dissented from the policy adopted by Mr. Glad- I stone—(cheers)—whose name did not appear to have lost its infloence in that part of Cheshire--(renewed cheers)— and of his government in respect to the establishment of a legislature in Ireland for the menagement of Irish affairs, but they had a natural desire to be informed whether they were prepared to support Lord Salisbury in the " do- nothing "policy that he sketched out at the Mansion House. or whether they had undergone the change that since the 9th of November had apparently come over the minds of Her I.ajesty's Government, and whether they were prepared to support a policy of repression, apart from and owithout any reference to remedial measures for Ireland. It would he a source of gratification to find indications of a ground of re-union among the scattered sections of the Liberal party, or if they found, as he was sure they would, ground for common action at least upon those matters on which they were agreed. As regarded the question of Ire- land, the Case was no doubt different, and it would be pre- mature to hope that a ground of common action could yet be found. But he did hope that those who had taken a separate course from the rest of the party in regard to that great question would feel the whole weight of reeponsibility which rested upon them. It was not many weeks ago since the Government were boasting of the improved condition of Ireland, and of the peace which reigned in that country. New the scene had changed. (Cheers.) These promises of tranquility, which were prompted by the mere fact that a Conservative Government had entered into office, had been proved to be unfounded, and at the present moment we. were brought fees to face with a condition of things which re- sembled very closely that which the country bad to deal with in the autumn and winter of 1880, after the rejection of the bill which was known as the Compensation for Dis- turbance 14ill. (Hear, hear.) Then, as now, the measure intended to check evictions in Ireland had been rejected ; then, as now, its rejection had been followed by the recru- descence of all the evils of the past, and the country was brought face to face with the prospect of a bad winter in Ireland. It could not be doubted that the immediate cause of this state of things was the rejection of the bill which was brought forward in the last session by Mr. Parnell. (Cheers.) It certainly appeared to him that there never was a period in which- it was of greater importance for the best interests of England and Ireland that there should he a quiet winter in Ireland than it was at the present time. (Hear, hear.) To check evictions, with all the excitement and anoer, and not infrequently the horrors, which accompany

them, seemed an object of priceless value to all men at the 'present moment; and he should have thought that if there were any persoue who ought to set a high value upon secu- rity, tranquillity, and calmness in Ireland now it was the party who put themselves forward especially as the de- fenders of the union. (Cheers.) Such a period would have been secered to it, at a moment of enormous importance, if Mr. Parnell's bill had been pissed into law last autumn. They now in Ireland had been brought back to that error and mistake that was made in the winters of 1880 and 1881. Now, how did the Government that was in power at that , time deal with that condition of affairs? They dealt with it by introducing a Coercion Bill on the one hand and remedial measures on the other. They dealt with it, indeed, upon the principle which Mr. Gladstone described the other day in the House of Commons as the principle if judicious mixture. (A laugh.) Well, what was the result? It had ultimately to be modified, and finally abandoned. Were they to recommence that course again? Were they to revert to what Lord Carnarvon celled the miserable habit of repression? Or were they to seek out some better .way of dealing with the evils of Ireland? (Cheers.) It now seemed as if the Government were about to revert to the path of repression, as if they were about, after hesitation and uncertainty, after going tort in one direction and then in another, after promising local self-goyernment for Ire- land through Lord Randolph Churchill, any sort of legisla- tion through Lord Salisbury, and a great deal of legislation ' through Sir Michael Hicks-Beaeh—(laughter)—and after haying boasted they had settled the Irish gnestion without repression and without asking for fresh powers—it seemed very mush as if they were reverting to the state of mind in which they were last January; and as if they should have, when Parliament met, to listen to another appeal similar to that which was made by the last G-overnment of Lord Salis- bury jest before its fall. (Hear, hear.) If they did resort once more to this line of policy the anti of such an attempt would once more be fraught with failure and discredit. No man, it might fairly be claimed, env attempted to carry out that kind of policy more honestly or snore justly than Lord Spencer, and yet he had come definitely to the conclu- sion, as a final result of his own experience, that there was no good to be got by a policy of that descliption. It was quite true that the present Government were at present only putting in force in Ireland the existing law, although it must be admitted that they bad had to go back five seri- taries for the purpose of finding a law suitable to their pur- pose. (Laughter.) They bad not yet, undoubtedly, an- nounced their intention of applying for increased powers, and it was quite possible that they might hope to escape the disagreeable necessity of ttoiag so; but the worst of it was that this path of repression led down a slip- pery incline, and that when once entered upon it was exceedingly difficult to stop. (Hear, bear.) They would find theinsetveS, if such a policy were perse- vered in once more landed in the weary round of hopeless and resuitlese coercion. But there was, apparently, another matter floating in the minds of some persons, which, per- haps, in the course upon which we were now just beginning to enter, might be nearer than maay supposed. He meant the suspension of the Irish members from their duties in Parliament, and the carrying out of vital legislation for Ire- I land in the absence of her representatives. When once they entered into-a contest of that descriptien, they were I bound to look at the possibilities that lie before them ; and ' what he welded to know was how it eonld possibly be con- templated with satisfaction by those who were eut-and'out defenders of the Act of Union that we should be in any de- gree approaching a state of things in which we should find ourselves legislating for Ireland with scarcely any Irish I members in the House of Commons. It was a very earnest conviction that it was absolutely necessary to ind out some better and wiser method of dealing with the difficulties of Irelaed than those which bad been followed with sush evil ' results in the past that induced the Government of Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—in the last Parliament to lay before the House of Commons and the public a plan for dealing with those Irish evils which they held would be successful in bringing them to a conclusion which appeared to them to be consittent with the great principles which had ever ac- tuated the Liberal party—the plan, namely, of allowing the Irish people to manage their own Irish affairs by the estab- lishment of an Irish legielature ie Dublin for the conduct of Irish legislation and administration. (Cheers.) They were not in the least insensible of the grievous condition of that social disorder which unhappily had existed in Ireland for a very tong tittle •' nor to the crimes and outrages which had too often marked the agrarian confliet which went on con- stantly in that country, but they were deeply convinced of the impotence of the methods which had been adverted to to eradicate those evils, and were bound to endeavour to find some other mode more likely to be crowned with suc- cess, by which they might not suppress for a time, but finally eradicate, these evils. For his own part he was convinced that the only final solu- tion of the great difficulty would be found in the adoption of the lines of policy proposed by Mr. Gladstone last year. Other plans wovld only resale in producing further lawless- ness, outrage, and crime. The new democracy of Great Britain was on its trial. The English and the Scotch peoole had not been directly responsible for the cruel misgovern- ment of Ireland in the past, but their responsibility now for evesy step that was taken with regard to that country would be of the strictest kind. (Hear, bear.) If the Gov- ernment were unable to offer any other methods of settling; the differences of Ireland, except those which former Gov- ernments have been in the habit of using with such signal and increasing failure, future historians would have to re- cord of their rule, as past historians had recorded of the rule of the classes which preceded them, that it had failed to produce the result of righteous Government—the happi- ness and contentment of the people. (Cheers.) He was very confident that it would not be so. The final settlement of that great question might be delayed for a time—with consequences which all good men must lament—but the day was not far distant when the British people, setting aside the miserable habit of coercion, would turn with well- founded confidence to the just and farasightki policy recom- mended to them by the greatest of livieg statesmen, which would alone, he believed, he truly worthy of a wise, a free and a generous nation. (Cheers.) Mr. E. R Russeen, M.P., who was loudly cheered, then addressed the meeting. He referred to the business that had been transacted at the afternoon conference. Referring to the resolution passed by the conference to the effect that the nation had had pretty well enough of the House of Lords, Mr. Russell asked, if we were to have a second chamber at all, what was it to be? (A. Voice: A repre- sentative chamber.) Well, it might be that if it were elec- ted upon a popular principle. He would accept it, but he must say if it were an assembly of superior persons only— (laughter)—he would much rather have the aid House of Lords. (Hear, hear.) They could apply the screw to the neeellouse of Lords when they wanted to de so, but he was afraid it would be a difficult matter if they bad a highly intellectual assembly chosen, because it was so vastly supe- rior to everything else that it would be impossible to con- vince them by mere popular pressure that they ought to go away. However, these were mere refinements of the ques- tion, which did not affect the strength of the resolution of the people of this country that the present state of things should not go on, and that either by an overruling veto, or some other method, they should constitute the House better, get better work, having less prejudice existing in it, and in this way effect a great and revolutionary change. The great subject of the moment was that of 'lreland. Upon such a matter as that Lord Ripon was no ordinary speaker. He had been in several Liberal Cabinets, and what was much better, he had always had a right to be in the most Liberal Cabinet that could be devised, because there never had been a time when he had not been at the extreme point of advanced opinion upon the great questions affecting the well-being of the country. (Cheers.) Lord Ripon had ca-operated with Mr. Gladstone, Lord Spencer, Mr. Morley, and the other members of the Cab- inet, in preparing and introducing to the nation the great measure in which was first embodied the general principle to which they pinned their faith as to the future improvement of the state of Ireland. Lord Ripon also told them, as they all knew, he was the intimate persenal friend of many of those distinguished gentlemen who were to meet on the morrow et tell them how not to do it. (Loud laugh- ter.) He said how not to do it, because that really seemed to be the be all and end all of their suggestions. (Laughter.) His feeling with reference to his own friends who were in the ranks of the Liberal Unionists was as if his old friends had forgotten to converse with him in his own language, and could only speak in some unknown tongue. He did not recognise their accents or the old spirit which animated their lives—that eager spirit for freedom and ad- vancement, and that candid generous allowance for the re- suit of ill-government, and that sense of historcal conse- quences of past Government iniquity, and the old feeling that only in sound Liberal principles was there hope for the future. All this had gone, and he heard language bard, cold, stony, icy; the language of more repression and the language of indifference, and he was constantly called upon to believe that the conditions of the Irish nation, which all his life he had been told by Liberal leaders were the consequence of past misgovernment and past evil, lay now in the malignant perversion of the Irish people. (Cheers.) He was not prepared for this, was not prepered to join in such conversation, or to hold out the right hand of friendship until the language of their old friends was very different and much more like what it used to be. (Cheers.) The great desire they ought to have in reference to Ireland was to raise its moral tone. They had the opportunity, as Lard /Upon had told them, two or three months agoond they missed it. What was that opportunity? It was the opportunity of solving by moral,legal.and judicial means, the problem which now stared them in the face every day. Mr. Russell sugge-ted that if the same set of conditions existed in this country as in Ireland, they would produce the same results. Undoubtedly good contracts would be evaded, the rights of landlords would be wrong- fully disregarded, and evil would creep in. But he conten- ded that the lawlessness of the Irish people had ctme to en- tertain in their ideas on the subject of land had not spread into other relations of life—(hear, hear)—that there IVA'S no class in Ireland giving business to the Divorce nourts— (great cheering)—and that the Irish people were religious, honest, and comparatively free from crime. In the course of trade they paid their way. Well, they ought to hey ery thankful for this, and they ought to be very careful how they trifled with the springs of human conduct. The whole situation could be described in the language of Long- fellow :

„ . With useless endeavour fer ever and ever . Is Sisyphus rolling his stone up the mourtain. This course of English policy had been very truly described to them that night by Lord Ripon. They had in their hands the means of altering the whole aspect of the state of things if the country could only be brought to see this, as he hoped it would, in the series of meetings with reference to this Question which it had been arranged by the National Federation to hold. It would only be giving to Ireland in- __

stitutions in accordance with her own views and under her own management, which would bring about her happiness, and remove from us what had hitherti been, and was likely to be, a very grave disgrace to our Empire. (Loud cheers.) Mr. C. H. Oeresaue, M.A., secretary to the Irish Protes- tant Home Rule Association, moved "That this meeting expresses its continued and unabated confidence in the Right. Hoe. W. E. Gladstone—(cheers)--es the leader of the Liberal party, and cerdially approves of the resolutions I adopted at this days' conference." There had beer, he said, a change in the disposition of England to Ireland, and of Ireland to England—(cheers)—and be would admit to the credit of English Liberals, that the first indication of change came from them. The English people were now disposed to govern Ireland according to the notions of Irish- men. (Cheers.) The best intelligence of England had failed to settle the Irish land question, and land at the pre- sent time was unsaleable on secount of the Act of 1881, which did not reach one-third of the tenantry, and which had failed because they had trical to settle the Irish question against the best opinion of Ireland. (Cheers.) If Emgland would admit the right of Irish opinion to influence the affairs of Ireland, then be would •oneeele for the mass o Irishmen that it was possible for Irishmen to deal with the needs of the country and develops their individuality within the lines of one great empire. (Cheers.) The Irish Na- tionalists were prepared to work with English Liberals to- wards that consummation, awl if God granted that then to Mr. Gladstone might all praise be given. (Loud cheers.) Sir B. W. Forma, who was cordially greeted, seconded the relsolatien, and said he was glad that that wise manage- ment which ,had always characterised Mr. Schnadhorst's work should have induced him to bring about a conference of the Liberal 4ssociations of that part of the kingdom in that division or that county. He hoped good things would come of it, and trusted they would send back to represent them in Parliament that good honest Radical, Mr. Brunner —(loud eheers)—who did them immense credit by his indus- try, his earnestness, his keen desire.to serve their interests in every opportunity. and who, above all, honoured them by the fidelity he showed to the great principles they sent him to represent. (Cheers.) The Conservatives, he continued, had been in power six months, and they had yet no plan to offer the country with regard to Ireland. He said that whilst they expressed confidence in Mr. Gladstone and his party, they had tbe right of Liberals to demand from the Conservatives what they were going to em. (Hear, hear.) The present Government were only in office as it were by the leave of a certain section of the Liberal party. and they held their position under a kind of supervision. Lord Ran- dolph Churchill had recently said that the guiding princi- ples of the policy of the Government would be to Preserve the Union of the Unionist party. (Laughter.) In other words, they wanted to keep their ticket of leave. (Re- newed laughter.) It might be very well for them to go on carrying oat a certain form of the Liberal policy in order to retain their position on the Treasury Bench ; but although the Liberals might be satisfied that they were advancing Liberal principles by adoptibg them and making it all the , easier for them when the time same te carry out the great reforms on which Liberals had set their hearts, yet they could not be satisfied to see them dodging the great respon- sibility of the Irish question. They could not be satisfied to allow them to remain there to carry out Liberal measures in their own form, for they believed that Liberal work was worthy the best hands that could be applied to it, and thee it should be undertaken by those gentlemen who for years had shown their devotion to Liberal principles, who formu- lated those reforms, as the result of honest study and honest inquiry into the wishes and aspirations of the people of this country. (Cheers.) Let them demand from the Tory party what their measures were, and if they were not satis- factory, then it was the duty of every honest Liberal to up- set that Government in order that righteousness might be carried out. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was carried with great enthusiasm. Mr. T. SNAPB, who was received with applause, moved "That this meeting expresses its high apprecistion of the character and public services of the most noble the Marquis of Ripon, K.G., and tenders to him, and also to Sir B. W. Foster, F.. R. Russell, Esq., M.P., and C. H. Oldham, Esq., !W.A., its hearty thanks for their attendance and for the speeches they have delivered." Mr. Snaps referred in complimentary terms to the gentlemen mentioned in the resolution. Mr. JAMES TOIMINSON seconded the motion, and referred with admiration to Lord Ripon's beneficial rule in India. He hoped that the aristocracy, who had upon the Irish ques- tion ranged themselves upon one side, would see the error of their ways, and act justly and righteously. He was con- vinced the Lords were standing in their own light, for if they never trused the people, how could they expect to be the trusted leaders of the people. (Hear, hear.) With time en their side, and with perseverence in well doing, the Liberal party would bring about a peaceful and permanent settlement of the Irish question. (Cheers). Mr. T. E. Eugs, M.P., who was loudly cheered, said he would merely paraphrase the resolution which he had the honour and pleasure to support. It was that they gave their + best thanks for the attendance and, the speeches of a Radi- cal marquis— (laughter)—a Radical doctor—(cNers)—one of the most brilliant and eloquent of English journalists, and one of the most eloquent of young Irishmen. (Cheers.) He thought there would be no lack of enthusiasm on the part of that meeting in giving their warmest and heartiest thanks to those four gentlemen. The Leeds Conference adopted ten or eleven Liberal reforms, and they had nailed three more colours to the mast that afternoon—and bad it not been for the adroitnesi of Sir Walter Foster, he believed several more would have been added. (Laughter.) The work which the democracy of this kingdom was giving to statesmen was increasing every day. One thing blocked the way, and that was the state of Ireland. They wanted once more the principle of freedom extended—freedom for Irishneen'to manage their own affairs. They had now in office a set of political tricksters (Laughter) These were backed and kept in office by a number of shaky and ricketty Liberals. (Laughter, and a Voice: " Capital.") There was, he believed, a salutary process going on. These shaky and ricketty Liberals were gradually stereotyping into Toryism. They wished Toryism to do whatever it could with them, for they only clogged their progress. There was another process going on. Not only were the shaky Liberals becoming Tories, but the Liberals were beccining Radicals, and what they in this country wanted was that this great work of church, of land, of education, and of lecal self-gov- ernment should be entrusted, not to the set of men now in office, but to men who were nobly represented by those four gentlemen, to whom ho asked them to give their heartiest and warmest thanks. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. The Marquis of RIPON, on rising to respond, was greeted with prolonged cheering. He thanked the meeting for the cordial manner in which they had passed the resolution, and concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the chair- man. They knew, he said, better than he did, Mr. Shaw's devotion to the Liberal cause. They had all seen how ably he had discharged his duties that evening, and he was per- fectly certain they would very readily accord him their hearty thanks. (Cheers.) Mr. SCHNIDITORST, in seconding the resolution, remarked the experience they had had that evening indicated that there was no need for discouragement in the Liberal party. (Heer, hear.) He was satisfied they might say as Mr. Glad- stone said some years ago with regard to the question of re- form, that "Time is on our side," and everything was working towards a seccessful issue of the great principles to which the Liberal party had committed it- self. (Cheers.) The vote was accorded with much enthusiasm, and Mr. Shaw having briefly replied, the meeting broke up.
TEBRIFIO GALE.-GREAT LOSS OF

LIFE. • There was a renewal on Wednesdiy night of the heavy gale throughout the country. The wind was very high and much rain fell, the barometer being at the lowest point touched for forty years. The captain and two of the crew of the fishing boat over- turned in the English Channel on Wednesday were washed ashore next morning between liythe and Sand•

gate. A woman named Ford was blown bv the gale against a wall at Northfield, Ilfracombe, on Wednesday night, and killed on the spot. At Ilfracombe, a woman was knocked down by the wind and killed on the spot. A railway waggon was also over- turned by the gale. Daring the storm a lady took refuge in an old castle at Ballemamore, near Kellasbee, county Longford. when the dilapidated building cellapsed through the force of the wind and killed her. During the storm on Wednesday night a chimney stack at Penclawdd :Tinplate Works, near Swansea, was blown down, killing two girls and a boy. The Cestletown (Isle of Man) lifeboat saved the crews of eight men of the trawler Swift, of Douglas, and the schooner Julia. bf Runcorn. The Tenby lifeboat saved the crew of three men of the ketch Honor, of Cardiff. The Thurso lifeboat saved the crews of eleven men of three vessels in Scrabster Roads—the Henry Florence, the Mar- garet Garton, and the Lyra. The Danmore, county Water- ford, lifeboat saved the crew of three men of the trawlec Agenora, of Tenby. A remarkable feature of the gale in Liverpaol was a tot. rifle taunderstorm, which passed over the city and suburbs early on Thursday morning. On Wednesday, a train upon the narrow gnage railway which runs between Festiniog and Pottmadoe, on the Welsh coast, was rounding a curve on the mountain side when it encountered the full force of the blest and was blown clean over. There were only a few paisengers, and they escaped serious injury. The brigantine William, of Drogheda, has been totally wrecked at Newcastle, county Down. The crew were saved. The severity of the gale lies been felt all along the Brit- ish Channel, and the damage done in Seuth Wales kas been very general. One death is rep,rted on Aberdare moun- tains. The mail train out of Aberystwith had to turn back, and the mail train from the coast section had to stop, at Tovryn, and as the line was deeraged by floods traips could not get through to Aberystwith until Thursday morning. There have been two or three wrecks in Cardigan Bay, but the crews were saved ey means of lines. " The through line of the Caledonian Railway was blocked for nearly three hours on Thursday morning, at elea.ttock by a goods train leaving the line because of the snow. The storm raged with unabated fury on Wednesday night and Thursday morning over thlr whole of the north of Ire- land. Telegrams from various parts of Ireland report a great amount of dam.ge. The damage d)no to property at Atby is almost unprecedented.

Lord Salisbnrr returned to London, on Tuesday, from visiting the Queen at Windsor. _
Mr. CnainlyerLain arid his party, now at Corfu, are ex- pected to reLoin to England about the 15th or 20th otant.

A Birminehere ley, named Bettersby, was killed at Derby on Sunday through being knocked down by a run+ away horse. ' Two women, named Wilkinson, mother and daughterorete 'on Monday found deed in their beds at Belfast. It is be- lieved they were tsuffocatod by fumes from a charcoal fire. The man Polgheetewhe was sentenced to death at the late Exeter Assswes, has had tie sentence commuted to penal sere vitude for life. Polglase killed a man whom he found eon- coaled in his hayrick- Only half a crown spent on a bottle of Bt. Togeler Company, sole proprietor, 44, tarrioodon-road, London. The smack Spark arrived at Yarmouth Harbenr on Mon- day with the lots of three of her crew. They were engaged ferrying fish to the rteem sorrier when the boat capaezed and they were drowned. The Prince and Princess of Wales and their guests Oft Sunday attended the re-opening by the Bishop of Nerwich of the Church of St. Peter, Wolferton, which has been re- stored from designs by Mr. Blomfield. The High Sheriff of Weetmoreland, Mr. E. 11. Wilson, died at hie prat, Dellem Tower, Millatherpe, on Wednese , day night. The deoeseed was the last male representative of a family connected with the county for five or six eine turies.

A CON-STAMM Sircereo-Early on Yonday morning, at Jarrow, Police-constable Dobbin finding the door of the County Hotel open, rapped at the window. The landlord, Mr. Robinson, came oat, drew a revolver, and fired, wound- ing the constable in the right arm. His wife and others per- suaded him to . desist from farther violence, and he was con- veyed to the police station. . At Cork, on Monday, Dr. Tanner, M.P., summoned Di's- • trict Inspector Milling, in (rennet:ion with the aeeault upon the former by the police. The court we crowded, amongst those present being Mr. O'Brien and several Irish members. After hearing the evidence, a majority of three out of five magistrates decided to commit Inspector Milling for trial on the technical charge of assault. MR. GLADSTONE AND TIM CLAIMS or IROLAITD.—Mr. Gladstone has sent the following reply to resolutions passed, at a recent meeting in support of Home Rule at the Can- greee Hail, Brighton :—I thank you for the intimation, you have kindly eonveyed. and am glad to hear each fresh instance of determined stunt to the equitable demands of Irelend, of which the concession will be eo advantageous to England." THE TITHE AGIT.LTIOX IN WILES.—Ths Ecclesiastienl Commissioners, who receive the largest proportion of tithes ' payable in the pules of Whitford, Ylintehire, have declined to grant any reduction in the tithe rents now due, and have served writs upon a number of farmers to receiver the amounts owing. It is expected that several distraiuts will be made, and that the agitation, which kad been dormant for some weeks, will recommence with great oigour. GREAT STRIKE 07 TIM-PIATX Ti'ONXIMS.—On Monday morning, in pursuance of a resolution paned at a delegate meeting on Saturday, the whole of the tinhoese abd mill- men engaged at the Nantygio, Blaine, Abertiliery, Pontet- mister, and Aberearn Tin-pleno Works in Monmouthshire ' gave notice to terminate all contracts by Tuesday night. The effect will be the reduction of output by 20,000 boxes ' per week, and the enforced idleness of several thousand worlepeople. Dressmakers cern bny no better rewing cotton ellen Dirostey sad Wright's, whin!, for eererseth is utteratealled.—Adert. SMITHFIELD Camreen Snow. The annual show of the Smithfield Club opened at the Agricultural Hall, London, • on Monday. The entries show a falling-off, but the quality of the exhibits is maintained. The Queen has been awarded the first prize for three-vea,r-ol d Devon steers, and a first for Devon steers between three and four year. The Prince of Wales is the winner of the first award for two-year-old shorthorn steers, and litr. David Pugh, M.P., is second in the same CIaSS. THE COAL TRADE.—A meeting of the representatives of coal owners awl workmen in the lf orthemberland coal trade was held at Newcastle on Petard:l, when a committee was appointed to consider the hest means of improving the trade in the district, which is at present very much depressed. The miners employed at the new Treclegar Collieries serteer , work on Saturday /lewdest a reduction of 24s per cent in the rate of wages. The strikes also continue at several other collieries, and upwards of 1,000 workmen have been thrown out of employment. A STORMY MFETINO.—A large meeting was held on Sun- day at Tinbalie, about a mile from Carrick-on-Suir. Con- tingents were present from Waterford, Kilkenny, and Tip- perary, and it was estimated that 10,000 attended. A large force of pence and milittry occupied a position outside the bounds of the meeting. Resolutions were pasted in support of Home Rule, denouncing evictions, supporting "the plan of campaign," end expreteing gratitude to Weesrs. Dillon and O'Brien. Occasion's' charges were made by the police, ' who were received with volleys of stonee. Local clergy- men, however, interfered and prevented any serious disturb- [ ance. 1 , kAPTURE OP A FORGER IN MANOMETER —At the Man- cheater City Police Court, on Tuesday morning, a man named George Tracey, known as William Edward Bailden, Arthur Foster. n Walter Nicholls, William Crawley, and Frank Falkla'ni. who is a convict license bolder, was placed In the dock on a charge of forgery, by which he obtained five thousand pounds. The prisoner is a middle-aged, cleri- cal-looking man. He was wanted in Birmingham for not complying with the conditions of his convict's license. Ten years ago, et Liverpool, he was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude, for a similar offence. Caminada applied that the prisoner should be discharged in order that he might be handed over to the London or Birmingham police. Thema- gistrates made an order to this effect. LORD SALISBURY AND COMING LEGISLATION.-011 Wed. nesday, Lord Selisbury was entertained by the City Con- eervative Club. In the course of aspeech, be acknowledged the support of the Dissentient Liberals on the Irish ques- tion, and said that the Government would not be anxious ea find occasions of difference with their friends. With regard to legislatioo, he annsunced that the Government desired to deal with local government for England and Scotland, and afterwards for Irelami. They also wished to amend the law relating to the transfer of land. He denied thet Conserva- tives had been blind to the advantages of extending munici- pal government to London outside the City, or that their views in regard to Parliamentary procedure had changed. He alsi called attention tothe nature of the present agita- tion ire Ireland. A CHRISTMAS PRESENT.-50 choice Cigars, in. bow, pent free, for is.—SvoLurr, Sankey-street, Warringieen.—Acht. A COMMEMORATIVE TOWER FOR LONDON.—We are in- formed that it is intended to construct a large tower in London in commemoration lot the jubilee year of her Majesty's reign. This tower is to be 440 feet high at the extreme top, and 420 feet at the top platform, from which may be seen eight or nice counties. It will overlook every other structure yet built in London. The base of the tower will be 75 feet square, and there wilt be a foundation of 25 feet. It is proposed to erect this structure at the top of Ox- ford-street, where the ground lies high, and it is expected that the work will be commenced in January neeet. The ironwork (of which there are some hundred tone) is placed in the hands of the Horsley Iron Company, Staf- fordshire, whose tender is LlO,OOO. We understand that. the name of the structure has not yet been decided upon— Iron. CHAMPAGNE FROM SAUMUR.—It is announced that the Gold Medal has been awarded to Messrs. Ackermen-Laurw ance at the Liverpool Exhibition for their Dry-Royal Cham- pagne. This Wins, of which one is reminded at almost every railway station in England, is now sold not only by Gilbey's Agents and the varieus Cenoperative Stores, but also by the old-fashioned wire merchants. The question naturally arises why the introduction of this wine should have met with such an unprecedented success, and it is not difficult to tied an answer ; for, in the first place there has for years been a want keenly felt in England for a pure Sparlelinie Wine of uniform Tenable quality and reasonable price. Secondly,no doubt, as the late Dr. Druitt said, it is , better to drink the finest wine produced in Seurnur than second rate Champagnes grove in the adjoining districts of Reims and Epernay, while it must be a boon to all con- sumers of Sparkling Wines to be able to obtain, at a mo- ment's notice, in every town and village, a bottle of really good Champagne for 3a—The Morning Post, December Btb, 1880, Tug CAMPBELL DIVORCE C•EF.—On Saturday, Mr. Finley, on behtlf of Lord Colin Campbell repu- diated the evidence as to his wife's condition before the mar- riage was consummated. Several witnesses were called to prove the visits of the Duke of Marlborough to Lady Colin Campbell ; and Alfred Davies, travelling servant, deposed that in May, 1584, he was in Paris, and watched Lady Colin, who was staying in the Hotel Continental. She left the hotel several times and met the Duke of Marllenrongle and another gentlemen at separate times. Lady Celle also went to the Hotel. Windsor. where he believed she wee in company with the Duke of lelarloorengh.—On Monday the witness Davis who had been etnployed to watch -Lady Colin 'Campbell's movement in Paris, was again Exemtned but the principal evidence was that of two brothers named Boyd, who had been rettined for the same purpose. Their statements generally were of an incriminatory character. The Duke of Argyll and Lord Colin Campbell' were also examined, the latter at great length, his seninuco to:1,11,1g to i, show that he hart suspected his hire almost from the first. His lordship's examination was not concluded wht a the couit adjourned until Wedneeday— On taking his seat on Wednesday in the Divorce Division Mr. Justice Batt intimated, with reference to the application on the previews day for security being given as to Lady Cohn Campbell's costs in the divorce suit, that he deolined to make any order at present, though he t oaght the matter should be reserved for coneiderstion hereafier. Lord C. Campbell gave further evidence in the Divorce Court, and said amongst other matrera that Lady Cohn admitted that while she was ill she had receered two or three letters daily . from Lord Blandferd. He denied the accusetiont made against him in regard to Mary Watson. and also that he had deputed Lady Miles to apelentise to Dr. Bird on his lehelf. He also gave further infeemation SS to the stateet his health, and said that from Augnet, 1883, to the m d ilo of 1885 Lady Colin was watched at home and *roan. div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 11, 1886.

Tim Dissentient Liberals are still dissen- tient. They have talked and dined together in the Metropolis, and the result of their delibe- rations is that they find themselves to-day quite as much opposed to Home Rule as they were during the heat of the election cam- paign, T is ,n vain that Mr. GLADSTONE, Mr. JOHN MORLEY, Lord SPENCER, and Lord RIPON have held out the right hand of fellow- shiP to them ; they will have no part or lot with the, Liberals in giving Ireland a Parlia- ment of her own. Indeed, rather than that, they are prepared to postpone legislation with the ardto Ireland, and they will try to keep present Government in office with that, if with no other, object. It becomes clear, from the speeches made at the Conference on Monday, that instead of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL having made a mistake, so far as Liberal Unionists are concerned, in suggest- ing that there is no pressing need to deal vviai the Irish question, the chances are that he on a hint which had been given him was actingratherthan on his own inspiration. Lord R as the leader of the New FourthAß TNPGaTr? YN: was, as might be expected of and cautious; but so radically to granting Ireland a legisla- tiveoh mp opposed courteous s he assernhlY, that he will not move a single step in that direCtiOil. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is in the same frame of mind, for, though he was not present at the Conference, he sent a telegram to the effect that there could be no discussion as to re-uniting with the Liberal party until "the defeated policy were frankly abandoned." This, as it seems to us, is pre- posterous. It is, to say the least of it, unrea- sonable to lay it down as a preliminary to discussion in a matter of dispute that one party to the controversy shall frankly abandon of his contention. Coming the very ground from Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, such a proposal is offensive in the extreme. Has he forgotten that in the debate on Mr. GLADSTONE'S Bill he said that give him the piinciple of Home Rule without the Bill and he would vote for

it? The Bill is gone; the only question now before the country is the principle of Home Rule, and yet Mr. CHAMBERLAIN himself coolly proposes that this principle should be abandoned as a preliminary even to confer- ence with the Liberal Unionists ! It will be noted, too, that the member for West Bir- mingham, unlike his leader, Lord HARTING- TON, still uses the word Separatist. He ought [to know that politicians who are as good [ Liberals and as good U nionists as he regard , the nickname as insulting. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN has not improved in any way by going [ abroad; he has rubbed shoulders with the Turk and has grown des', )tic. Let us be thankful that Lord HARTINGTON has re- mained at home, where there is so much to remind him that he is an English gentleman. So far from being indifferent about irritating the Liberals as a party, he takes pains to be at all times respectful, and is moreover anxious to make it appear that the Liberal Unionists are the true Liberals. But in this he is far from successful. He admits that if the Government bring in a measure for Ireland which stops short, as it probably will, of Home Rule, it will not satisfy the bulk of the people l; Ireland. He himself is not disposed to listen to the voice of the Irish people, and it is just because he halts on the way in a matter of this kind that he cannot be regarded in this case as true to Liberal principles. There is nothing new in this; Lord HARTINGTON was always somewhat disposed to hang back. Twenty years ago he was amongst those who were not prepared to concede household suffrage; and it is little more than twelve months since it was an open question with him whether it would be wise to confer the same franchise upon Ireland as upon the rest of the King- dom. What is new, is his allowing himself on the proble-n of the Government of Ireland to get so far behind. He is not, to be sure, so much of a Rip Van Winkle as Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN not long since made him out to be; but we are inclined to think he has been brought to take too gloomy a view of things as the out- come of his connection with Mr. GOSCHEN —the Skeleton of the Feast. Lord DERBY, speaking at the banquet which followed the Conference, said they opposed Home Rule "not as a measure which they considered merely rash or hazardous, but as in its nature essentially reactionary." In what way reactionary his lordship did not deign to explain; but he did proceed to say as to the national party, that "they were not to be trusted in this matter, and still less were they to be trusted with absolute power over a minority of their countrymen." "Not to be trusted "—that is the word ; it is an old phrase, and ore upon which the changes have been rung a hundred times,and in a hundred ways, whene .er a measure has been before Parliament wh;ch would have the effect of putting more pow in the hands of the people. It is a phrase which defines broadly 'lie difference between Liberalism and Toryism; the Liber - have faith in, the Tories distrust, the people. The reac- tionary politicians are those who, having fought within the ranks of the Libe:al party, refuse to respond to the call of their leader, when he bids them advance and trust the people of Ireland. They are the men of little faith who are so blind that they cannot ' see that Coercion has failed for two genera- tions and that the time has come to try Con- ciliation. The Liberal Unionists stand still, and ally themselves with the Classes; the Liberal party moves on in alliance with the Masses. " The powers that be" are for the moment masters of the situation ; but as Byron has it : I think I her a llitl,e bird which sings, Tr te peoplc) by-ami-bye will bo tin s'aonger.

THE holding of a Town's Meeting in Warrington to consider)the advisability ofl making the Warrinzton Library a Free Lend- ing Library has, as our readers are aware, been delayed through the illness of the Mayor (Dr. MACKIE). Meantime the Deputy- Mayor (Alderman HARRISON) has been called upon to act in such an emergency as has, un- happily, arisen, and it is understood that he will fix the meeting, and preside on the occasion. It will be held, in all probability, the Gaiety Theatre, the Public Hall being otherwise engaged, and, judging from the interest which has been shown in the question, and from the fact that over 400 burgesses and inhabitants, signed the re4uisition to the Mayor, it is likely to be well attended. It would be seen from the Mayor's letter to the members of the General Purposes Committee, on the course Warrington might take in cele- brating the QUEEN'S Jubilee, that the pro- - posal to male the Lending Library free to the public stands in the front rank. Certainly, nothing could be done that would be so generally approved, or that would be more likely to be of immediate and permanent benefit to the people. Apart altogether from the ques- tion of celebrating the QUEEN'S Jubilee, it is a step which must be taken, if Warrington is to keep pace with her neighbours who have the advantage of free Lending Libraries. To say nothing of parents, there are thousands of scholars whose &Ideation might be im- proved after leaving school; and, as a means to this end, the Lending Library, as in other towns, should be free to all corners. It is not sufficient to say, as is sometimes said, that those who will not pay a trifle over a penny per week do not care for books. If a boy went to the Library with twice the sum in his hand he would not be allowed to take a book home to read. He must present himself with a quarter's subscription—with at least eighteen pence—before a book can be lent him; and there is no denying that this is a great bar to the use of the Library. Evidence of this is furnished by the fact that there are but a few hundreds of subscribers in a town 0145,000 inhabitants. And, instead of in- 33.sing with the growth of the town, the number of subscribers is diminishing. Two years ago the annual income from sub- scriptions was ['7s; but for the year ending in March last it was [132 only. There has been a falling off of over twenty per cent. ; and what does this mean, seeing that in the same two years there has been a considerable ad- dition to the population? It means that the subscription is a prohibitive barrier which, these hard times, is shutting out, as it has always shut out, not only the really poor, but many who have hitherto been able to spare the amount required. Granted that if the subscription was abolished, and there was nothing to take its place, the Library Co rn- mittee would have to retrench. Even that would be better, with the Lending Library free, than the present unsatisfactory system. Other towns manage to provide Free Lending Libraries out of a penny in the pound on the rates. The inhabitants pay the penny rate in Warrington—they have been paying it for over thirty years—and it is natural, after waiting so long, that they should want to see the Lending Library of Warrington as free as are the Public Librar- ies of St. Helens, Wigan, Runcorn, South-

port, Blackburn, Bolton, and scores of other places. There can be no objection, of course, to making the way easy by providing, as the MAYOR is known to have suggested, ' a Jubilee Free Lending Library Fund, the interest of which might be applied towards meet- ing any deficiency arising from the abolition of the subscription system. It would be money ! well given and well spent; it would be a celebration of the Queen's Jubilee worthy of ! Her Majesty and worthy of the town, for it would take away a reproach, and be a con- stant and ever-increasing blessing to the people.

* * SHEET ALMA.N.A.O.—AIong with our next paper, there will be presented to each of our readers a large sheet Almanac, printed in two colours, and containing a large amount of local and general information. It will be adorned with a beautiful view of Winmarleigh House and an excellent por- trait of Lord Winmarleigh. Presented NEXT WEEK. Order early of newsagents. Examiner and Almanac—price one penny. The large sale of the paper on Almar Day affords a special opportunity to .ad vertisers. ESLEYAN MUSICAL FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN. Our advertisement columns contain a notice of this festival, which will be held in the Public Hall, on Monday evening. EXPLOSIVE STORE.—Meers. J. and T. Handley, quarry owners, Weston, were granted by the Runcorn magistrates on Monday the renewal of their license to store explosives at Weston. A RUNCORN PATENT.—Letters patent have been issued to Messrs. G. L. Wigg, M. Steele, M.D., and W. J. Wigg, for improvements in plant or apparatus to be used in the treatment of residuals from copper works and chlorine manu- facture to obtain pigments and sulphate of lime. FIRE AT A RUNCORN WORKS.—A large tar pot need for tarring ropes accidently caught fire at the works of the late Mr. Thomas Norman, Old Quay, on Monday. The fire bri- gade was quickly on the spot, but. their services were not re- quired, as the fire was smothered by means of planks cov- ered with sand being placed over the pot. A considerable number of pipes were smashed, but the damage is very light. MISAPPROPRIATION OF MONEY AT RUNCORN —Before Mr John Bruadrit and Mr. James Handley, at the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, James Cranks was charged with appropriating to his own use 17s, belonging to Joseph Oates. It was iroved that the prisoner had been entrusted with the cash to buy some ropes, but had spent the money on his own account, but he was sentenced to fourteen days' hard labour.

LICENSING MATTERS AT RUNCORN.—The Runcorn magistrates on Monday granted the transfer ef the follow- ing licences :—Brunewick Vaults, Brunswick, from Thomas Caldra to James Castles; the Welsh Harp, Cooper-street, from William Waterworth to Samuel Brown. Robert Baguley was granted temporary authority to sell at the Queen's Head, High-street. Robert Gorst, confectioner, High-street, was given permission to sell beer and wins at theishop recently occupied by Miss James. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—CoIoneI Ash- ton presided over the meeting held at Datton Workhouse on Tuesday. In reply to Mr. Aaron, the Clerk said the money due to the Authority by the Mersey Salt and Brine Com- pany, Weston Point, had not been paid, but no action was taken in the matter. The mosey due is the Company's proportion of the cost of making a sewer. The Inspector (Mr. Farrington) was directed to confer with the agent to Aston estate, with a view to obtaining an improved water supply for Bartineston. DROWNING FATALITY AT WlDNES.—Yest,nday morning, Thomas Perry, a sailor on board the steamer Kangaroo, of Deuglas, Isle of Man, was drowned in the West Break Dock, where the vessel is lying. Perry handed the mate a bucket of water from the dock side, and the mate placed the fluid in the water cask. When he returned with the empty bucket, Parry was nowhere to be seen, but half-an-hour afterwards his cap was found floating in the water, and his dead body was recovered with the grappling irons shortly afterwards. It is supposed that the deceased was pushed into the Dock by a crane that was at work where he was standing. MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES.—The annual meeting in connection with the Widnes Branch of the Wesleyan Foreivn Missionary Society, was held in Victoria-road Chapel, on Tuesday evening. There was a fail attendance and Mr. R. Shaw presided and delivered an address. The Rev. W. Wilson, chairman of the Liverpool district, des- cribed the labours of a Missionary in the Fiji Islands, and advocated the claims of the Missionary Society. The repert read by the Rev. J. Bryant showed that during the past year £l4l had been collected in the Widnes circuit. The collections for the Sunday's services and that evening amounted to .Cl 9. ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES.—Whilst assisting to pall down a large iron column amongst the debris at the new works of Messrs. Math ieson and Co, on Wednesday, John Hindley. 40 years of age, of Duke's Field, Runcorn, received severe internal injuries. The column fell upon him. He is at the Accident Hospital, Whines, in a pre- carious condition, under the care of Mr. Richards, assistant to Dr. McDonnell.—James Coason, 2,11 years, was seriously scalded on Wednesday, at his parent's house in Water- street. Whilst his mother was engaged about her house- hold duties, the boy seized a tea pot containing tea almost at boiling point and drank from the spout, scalding his throat and lining of his stomach. Dr. Hutchinson is in attendance oar the child. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—At the fortnightly meeting, held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, under the presidency of Colonel Ashton, the Clerk (Mr. H. Linaker) stated he had received a petition from the Prescot Guardians asking the support of the Board to a petition it was intended to send to the President of the Board of Trade in respect to the distress caused amongst the watchmakers of Prescot by the placing of foreign works in English Hall-marked cases. The petition asked that these foreign watches should not be palmed off on the public as English manufacture. It was ultimately decided, on the proposition of Mr. E. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Hadfield, that a supplementary petition should be presented to the Board of Trade. There INele he other business of interest. %VIM., FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.—A meeting was held at Alforde Chambers, on Wednesday afternoon, under the presidency nf Mr. H. W. Deacon, and there were pre- sent 'Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, Morrison, Carey, Brown, S. Robinson, S. T. Allen (clerk to the Local Board) and Lancaster (Librarian to St. Helens Corporation). Mr. Rothwell, contractor for the erection of the public offices, reported that he would have finished his work in connec- tion with the Library by Christmas Day. The tender of Mr. T. Sadler for the fittings of the Library was accepted. It was decided to leave the selection of books to a sub- committee, consisting of the Chairman, Mr. S. Robinson, and Mr. J. Morrison; and it was resolved to expend the £lO9 presented by Mr. J. T. Brunner. of Northwich, in the purchase of scientific books, to be called the "Brunner Collection." WIDNES PETTY SESSION:.—On Thursday, Mere Mr. E. K. Muspratt and Mr. T. S. Timmis, Luke Kelly, Edward Barrett, and James Taylor were each fined for drunkenness. For creating a breach of the peace in Midwood-street, Eliza- beth Dudley was bound over to be of good behaviour for two months.—Ann Johnson for a like offence committed in James-street, West Bank, was also ordered to find sureties.— Margaret Kerley, a young woman, was ordered to find sure- ties to keep the peace, or go to gaol for seven days for as- saulting a girl named Bridget Brennan.—Mary Ann Rock, who keeps an "oyster shop" in Widnes-road, was charged under two informations with having kept her shop open for the sale of oysters after the hour of 11 on the nights of the 24th and 25th ult. Inspector Wood stated the woman not having a refreshment license could not keep open after 10 o'clock. A fine of 2a 61, and costs us 61, was imposed in each case. POPULAR CONCERT AT RIINCORN.—The third• of the series of the admirably arranged concerts in connection with the Mill Brow Brass Band was held in the Public Hall on Saturday evening. The excellence of the programme and the low price of admission merited a much better at- ten lance of the townspeople. The programme included vocal contributions by Miss Wright, Miss Clara Taylor, Mr. T. Clegre and Mr. John Holford. Miss Taylor made a successful debut. Possessed of a contralto voice of great purity, she sang with, expression and artistic taste, and was twice recalled. Miss Wright contributed several songs with her accustomed ability with gratifying results. Mr. John Holferd was in capital form, and Mr. Clegg, who has a good bass voice, had to respond to an encore. The instru- mental selections by the band were most enjoyable items, and included solos by Mr. Outhwaite and Mr. R. Pierpoint, which were much appreciated. An interesting feature dur- ing the evening was the conjuring performances of Mr. Henry Hellier. Master Clifford Le Canteur acted as accom- panist. RuNcorm BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the cemetery on Wednesday. Mr. W Little pre- sided, and there were present Messrs. G. Moss, H. Coleburn R. Morris, W. H. Rogerson, and W. F. Salkeld (clerk). It was reported that the interments for the eight months end- ed Nov.'2sth were 210, a 'decrease of 5 on the correspond- ing period of 1885. The fees received for the same period amounted to £204 18e 6d, a decrease of £l5 193 6d. The report of the Finance Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr. Moss, showed that £lOO had been received from the overseers, and that the sum of £127 had been invested in 3 per cent. consols towards the sinking fund on the cemetery. The committee had given some consideration to the ques- tion of ecclesiastical burial fees, and found it necessary to aweit the arrival of the new vicar before coming to any conclusion.—Mr. Coleburn said the other Saturday after- noon his sister, Mrs. Blakemore, who is a widow, came on a visit to the town from Tranmere, and placed a beautiful wreath of flowers on a grave at the cemetery. Next day, the flowers had disappeared, evidently having been stolen. He mentioned the matter to show the public that these things were noticed. WIDNES ELOCUTIONARY AND AMATEUR DRAMATIC SO- CIETY.—The committee of this society gave an entertain- ment on Monday evening in the Baths Assembly-room, which had been lent free of charge by Messrs. Gaekell, Deacon, and Co. Although the gathering was confined to members and a few frieeds, the room was comfortably filled, and a musical and dramatic entertainment of a most enjoy- able nature was listened to. Miss James, Miss Leather- barrow, Mr. Webster Williams, and Mr. Joseph Morrison were responsible for the vocal part of the programme, and acquitted themselves to the evident satisfaction of those present. Miss James's contribution was a song entitled "The token," written by Mr. H. W. Cookson, and wedded to tasteful music by Mr. A. R. Sutton. Mr. H. Wade Deacon and Mr. Richard Lewis displayed their admir- able elocutionary abilities in the " Relief of Lucknow " and " The execution" respectively. Messrs. A. R. Sutton and F. Booth executed a pianoforte duet in good style. The con- cluding portion of the entertainment was the performance of the one act comedietta "Cut off with a shilling." The parts were taken by Miss Oakden and Messrs. H. W. Cook- son and Charles Nickson, and the several impersonations fully merited the warm plaudits bestowed upon them. The piece was staged under the direction of Mr. James White,. the stage manager. A vote of thanks to Mr. F. H. Gossage, who had fulfilled the duties of chairman, brought a most pleasant entertainment to an end.

MUNIFICENT Gin.—Sir Anflrew Barclay Walker has annowaced his intendon of presenting a sum of £15,000 to the Liverpool University College in com- memoration of the Jubilee year. •The money . will be devoted to the erecdon and fitting up of -a suite of engineering laboratoriei. ADMINISTRATION ORDER.—At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, a maniPeter Kenny,who said that he was a dresser of iron castings, employed at Mr. Slee's Works at Eariestown, applied to his IHonour Judge Ffoulkes for an administration order. lApplicant, who said that his wages were 245. a week, attributed his being in difficulties to the drunken habits of his wife. lie had kept a shop, with an off beer licence, but he gave it up about. 18 months ago. •Hi 3 wife had the management of the; shop. He sold the furniture of his house, and the shop fittings were given to the landlord in lieu of money due to him. Mr. H. L. Riley, who appeared for Leveral creditors, said that they. did not object t 3 a reasonable order. His Honour granted the order, directing that Kenny should pay 12s. a month. Kira Compourcs or LrwszEn. Aniseed, Benege, Tolu. with Ohlorodyne. tkd, Is Ltd, 2s 9d, of Chemists.— Advt.

IWIDNES COUNCIL GF EDITCATION.—We hold over until our next issue a report of the meeting of this organisation, which was held on Thursday evening. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR WlDNES.—Yester- day, Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest at the New Inn, Ditton, respecting the death of Police Sergeant Coutts. It appeered that the deceased on Monday night, at half-past ten, visited the constable at Farnwortb, and left him to walk horns across the fields. On his way he would have to cross the Ditton level crossing on the Cheshire Lines Railway, and sear that spot his dreadfully mangled body was found scattered about midnight. Ihe jury returned a verdict of " Acci- dental death," ttnd expressed the opinion that the driver of the train ought to have stopped where the accident occurred. They also recommended that an overhead bridge or a sub- way should be made at the crossing. PROPOSED GYMNASIUM FOR WIDNES.—Last night a com- pany of athletes from the Liverpool Gymnasium gave -an assault-at-arms in the Widnes Drill Hall. The object of the performance was to raise funds towards the cost of for- ming a gymnasium in the town under the aus- pices of the National Recreation Society. Mr. A. Alexander, F. R. G. S.. director of the Liver- pool Gymnasium, directed the clever and interesting evolutions of the young gymnasts, and they were frequently loudly applauded. Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., occu- pied the chair, and announced that Mr. Alexander had decided to form one under the auspices of the National Association. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Alexan4er at the close. WIDNES STARR-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—Under the auspices Of this society a concert was given in Lacey- street Wesleyan Schoolroom on Wednesday evening. Mr. T. C. Edwards-MOW., M.P.; occupied the chair, and the room was crowded. In the course of his opening speech, the Chairman said he did not think the benefits and advantages of Starr-Borkett Building Societies were sufficiently well known amongst the people, because if the principles of the societies were better known he was satisfied they would be taken greater advant ige of. (Applause.)—leurieg the even- ing Mr. J. Collins, of Bolton, delivered a lecture on the principles of Starr-Bowkett Building Societies. The pro- gramme included songs by Miss Annie Williams and Messrs. F. Scott, Bate, Eaton, tuson, and Ware. Two appropria- tions were made, and resulted in Mr. Evan Cross, grocer, of Penketh, being entitled to £4OO and Mr. John Jolley clerk, Cow-lane, Ditton, to £3OO free of interest for 12.,, years. The chairman and several other persons took up shares in the society. THE PLASTERER'S STRIKE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. E. K. Muepratt and Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, the master of the plasterers at the new public offices applied for a warrant against one of the men on strike. The men, he said, were threatening and interfering with others who wished to start work at the place, and were rendering the progress of the work innpossible.—lnspector Wood deposed that the plasterers had been on strike three weeks, and police officers had to be stationed near the buildings.—Mr. Muspratt said the Bench thought the ap- plication a very serious one. What ,the master wished to do was to put some of the men on strike into gaol without their having a proper trial. There ;were other legal means of deeling with the men, and what the magistrates wanted to know was why he did not act by such means in the first place. Their advice was that he should proceed by sum- mons, and then if that would not do, he could take out warrants. It was better that the applicant should go to a little trouble than send the men for trial. FELONIES AT Wentegs.—Michael Doyle, a labourer, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday charged with stealing £6 2s 2d, the property of Nicholas Killalea. The men lodged together at a common lodging-house in Lugsdale-road. On Saturday night Killalea placed his money in his trousers pocket, and placed the trousers under his pillow. Next morning, when he awoke, the trousers were on the floor and the money gone. He accused prisoner, who had get up two hours earlier, of the robbery, but he denied all knowledge. When threatened with imprison- ment he pulled 2s oitt of his pocket, and said Killalea ought to he thankful he had got that. The prisoner was see- tenced to a month's hard labour —James Lewis, labourer, Bear-street, defended by Mr. Knowles, was convicted of stealing a cock, worth is Cpd, the property of John Barton, greengrocer' ' Peel-street, and he was fined 20s and costs or a month's hard labour.—Mary Moran, a woman of no fixed residence, was charged with stealing a can, worth 11d, the property of Patrick Grady, 38, Greafell-etreet, from the Sun Inn. GUN WITHOUT A LICRNSE.—Charles Russell. labeeter, was summoned before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds to answer a charge of using a gun without hav- ing a license. Mr. Heal, supervisor of Inland Revenue prosecuted, and stated that between twelve and one o'clock noon on the 22nd October Samuel Hall and his wife, who live in Surrey-street. saw the defendant fire the gun twice in a field at Weston Point. A flock of pigeons was passing overhead, and one of the birds was killed and another wounded. The defendant placed them in his pocket.—These facts were proved.—The defendant stated that he had had a gun in his possession for over two years, and totally denied the allegation made in the charge. He called John Nick- son, farmer's son, who deposed to bearing a gun fired, and running out of the stables he saw a man pick up a bird. When the man saw him he ran away. Witness followed on, and when he got to Wilson's farm the defendant was gettiug his diner.—Charles Wilson, Greenway-road, stated that the defendlnt had not his gun on the day in question. —A fine of .£1 and costssEl, was imposed, or in default a month's hard labour. ST. PAUL'S WESLEYAN CRAM, RUSTCORI4,--00 Thurs- day evening Mr. John Simpsou iuvited the members Or t;1,; aorigreal.n -ti0r11314139*, St. Paul's Chapel to a tea meeting, of which he defrayed the cost, in Brunswick School. About 400 persons sat down to the repast, and at the public meeting held subsequently, the room was crowded. The Rey. George Wood, the superintendent of the circuit, presided. Mr. Simpson, as the senior circuit steward, explained that they were in financial difficulties, and the congregation had been called together to discuss the mat- ter. He should shortly be giving up his position of circuit steward, and he wished his successor to have a fair start and not be encumbered with a debt. The circuit debt, so far as he was able to ascertain, would at the end of the year amount to upward of £lOO. This he would pay off him- self. (Loud applause.) But they had other duties to per- form, and he urged noon them the necessity for indi- vidual effort so that their work would be more successful than hitherto. (Applause.) Although he was resigning his office of circuit steward he did not intend to slacken his efforts to promote the work of God in the Runcorn circuit, and promised to render what assistance he could. (Loud applause.)—Messre. J. R. Frith, B. Kniveton, and T. Sirnis- ter also delivered vigorous speeches. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. W. Simpson for his kindness in providing the tea, and for his generous offer to clear off the circuit debt. A HOUSEHOLD TYRA/CZ' AT RUNCORN.—Joseph Hoplev, a farm labourer, who lives in Surrey-street, appeared at Run- corn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of assault- ing his wife Ellen. Superintendent Hollingsworth asked the defendant, who by his appearance and manner was evi- dently under the influence of drink, where he had been. "I have been in the sun," was the reply, and there was loud laughter in court. With easy carelessness the defend- ant admitted that he had unlawfully beaten his wife. The complainant said she had come before the magistrates in order to get peace and quietness, for she bad had little dur- ing the past seven weeks. The defendant thought nothing of hiceing over the table and breaking the things. For three or four nights each week she da,e not take off her clothee and go to bed because of his violence. She did not think that he had been home sober one night during the past seven weeks. On the night of the Ist December he thrashed her and knocked her down, and sbe was uncon- scious until some neighbours attended to ber. Next morn- ing, whilst she was on the sofa "ton sore to turn over " he repeated his vlob-nce.—The defendant asked if sh did not give him dry peas for his tea.—The witness replied that barn end peas had been prepared for his dinner. If he came home at mideiebt she had to bring his dinner en the ttble'to show that it had been 111,11.. Witness in reply to the Bench, seid she would like a separation if something were allowed for the children. He was a labourer at Savage's farm and received Pe per week.—The Bench im- posed a fine of 208, and costs lOs tsi, or in default mouth's bard labour. He would also be bound over to keep the peace for six months. The defendant threw the amount of the tine on the table with a clatter, and turning to his wife said " That would buy you a good many shawls, wouldn't it." (Laughter.) Sale at LIA.YNES'S of Boots and Shoes, to make room for winter goods-42 and 44, Horsemarket-street.—Aatt. Trr-g MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. —An influential meeting -was held at Manchester Town Hall, on Thursday, to receive the report of the Consultative Committee appointed to investigate the Ship Canal scheme at the time it failed to obtain the necessary capital. Mr. Goldschmidt, ex-Mayor, said the com- mittee was entirely independent of the Canal Com- pany, and some of them at first adverse to the scheme, but they had unanimously signed the re- port recording their opinion that the canal was a sound undertaking. In the report they sent out they stated that they believed the works practica- ble, from the engineer's point of view, that they could be completed for £5,750,000, and that the pro- ject would speedily become remunerative. The committee finally said it was necessary before the issue of any further prospectus, the directors should be reconstituted and greatly strengthened. THE COUNTY COURT FOR WIDNES.—His Honour Judge Thompson sat at the St. Helens County, Court, on Wednesday, for the last time this year. Up to the present Widnes actions have been heard at St. Helens, but commencing in January next the new arrangement for holding courts at Widnes will come into operation. For the townships of Windle Eccleston, Parr, Sutton, Bold, Rainhill, Present, Hue-- ton ,Roby, Knowslev,Whiston, Rainford, and Tarbock, a-court will be held., as hitherto, on the second and fourth Wednesday in each month at St. Helen: but for the townships of Widnes, Crouton, Ditton', Hale, Halewood, Speke, and Woolton, a court will be held on the last Friday in each month at thel Police Court, Widnes. This will be a great con- venience to the solicitors and general public of the Widnes district, who had presented a petition on the subject to the Lord Chancellor, through their representative, Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss. PRINTING OF EVERY DESCRIPTION, executed by John S. Green, Printer. Bookseller, and Stationer, 34, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt.
