div.p: ENTERTAmmErrr AT Cnorr.—An entertainment • was given on Saturday evening by the members or the Croft Drum and Fife Band and their friends, at the Board, Schools, before a crowded audience, inn aid of the funds of the band. The Rector (theßeY. T. P. Kirkman) presided, and an interesting pro- gramme was gone tnrough in an excellent manner, under the conductorship of the Mr. F. W. Ball, the bandmaster, who also accompanied the various songs on the harmonium. At the conclusion of the entertainment the Chairmen proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Ball, and to the members of the band and their friends for their services, which was heartily accorded, as well as a vote of thanks to the Rector for presiding. TITHE AGITATION AT BITIITONWOOD.—A meeting* of farmers was held in the Chapel House Inn, Bur- tonwood, on Tuesday evening, to take into conside- ration the question of the payment of tithes, andto seek for a reduction thereof. he tithes around. Burtonwood, it may be mentioned are collected by the Rector of Warrington.—Mr. Forshaw, of Bur- tonwood-Brewery, was voted to the chair, and, in introducing the question, said the priceiof farm produce being so low, they thought it best to ask their worthy Rector if he could make a reduction in the tithe charges. Having given figures to show the cost of cultivating the land, he said that alto- gether he considered farmers were working at about .E 1 lOs per acre of a loss. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. J'. L. Stelfox (secretary of the Warrington Farmers' Club) said it had been mentioned so often that really it was as well known as the alphabet that farming did not now pay, and when it was said that farming did not pay, it required to be under- stood why it did not pay. The farm produced a certain amount of produce. which was sold at a certain price. It need not be brought more plainly before them that when the produce of the land was sold, only to pay the cost of produc- tion, it was incumbent upon farmers to consider whether a saving could not be brought about. While perfectly kind and cordial in their demeanour to the Rector, it would not be out of place to bring to the notice of that gentleman what tithes were. The tithe had now become •a tax upon labour, and if the clergy maintained their full Flaim to the title of tithe they would be losing what they might retain, and in grasping for the shadow lose the whole of it. (Applause.)—Mr. James Warburton, Dallam, said it would ill become him to sit still and not coincide with everything that had been said. Mr.`Stelfox had studied the question from beginning to end, and he did not think there was anyone in the room who would not endorse what he had stated. (Applause.)—The Chairman then moved "That the Rector be asked to make a reduction of 20 per cent. in the tithes, in consequence of the low amount realised for farm produce."—Mr. John Warburton, Dallam, in seconding the motion, said he thought there was no one present who would not coincide with him in saying the reduction was very much needed at the nresent time. (Applause.)—On being put to the meeting, the resolution was carried unanimously.—Mr. John 'Warburton, Dallam, moved "That a petition be draw n up, and sent by the whole of the tithe-payers of the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire, requesting Mr. Legh, M.P., to bring forward or support any bill or measure for the readjustment of the tithes in the coming See- sion of Parliament."—Mr. W. Haslam seconded the •motion, which, on being put to the meeting, was carried unanimously.—The proceedings then termi- , nated.

THE DESERTED HUSBAND AND HIS SEWING • MACHINE. William Peacock, of Greenway-road, appeared -before,the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, in the endeavour to ob- tain a sewing machine from the possession of the police. His wife eloped with another man eometime ago, and he , missed the machine, which was subsequesirly found in the house of Mrs. Howard, who also lived in trreenway-road.— Mrs. Howard replied that on the 9th July Mrs. Peacock en- • tered her house crying bitterly and asked her to buy the machine, as she had not sufficient money to go to her sister's. As the woman appeared distressed, she paid her £4 for the machine, and as she had bought it honestly she either wanted the machine fret:a the police, or the money. —Mr. Johnson (deputy-magistrates' clerk) : Why don't yon prosecute your wife for stealing the machine.—Peacock: I have found out that she is in America. She went away with Thomas Woodward, who lodged with this old woman (meaning Mrs. Howard.)—Mr. Johnsom said the machime could not be given up until the matter was properly settled. —Peacock said his wife did not sell the machine for muck, as she bad drawn all his money out of two banks. This woman" knew all about it.—Mrs. Howard: This woman did not know anything about it—Peacock throw a paper purporting to be a receipt for the payment of the machine by him on the table.—The Bench declined to make an order.

div.head: STORM AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES!
div.p: STORM AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES!

THREE MEN DROWNED A etcilffl v. PVCCcling violence swept over the dis; tricts of RunCnrn and Widnes on Wednesday_ night. Hail and rain desCfinded in torrents, and vivid light- ning flashes and loud peals of thunder were fre-; quent. The gale continu. ed. "Mout abatement on Thursday, and many exciting scenes We're witnessed on the river, and unhappily were attended with loss of life. While proceeding to Runcorn, the crew of the Bridgwater Company's steamer Bridgewater observed a sunken flat near to the West Slip with several men clinging to the rigging. The master of the steamer, Griffith Jones, immediately turned the steamer towards the flat, which was found to be the Dan, laden with sand, belonging to Messrs. Hill and Grundy, of Liverpool. The captain, named Robert Holden, and his son, also named Robert Hol- den, both living at Penketh, near Warrington, and a young man named John James Whaling, aged about 25, who lived with his parents at 65, Beau- mont-street, Widnes, were clinging to the boom, while another son of the captain, named James Hol- den, was in the rigging. The waves were washing over the men, and they appeared to be exhausted from the exposure to the cold, and before the three men on the boom could be reached they were washed away and drowned. The ,crew of the Bridgewater threw James Holden a rope, and he was dragged. on board the steamer in a weak condition. His legs had been chafed by the rigging until they were literally raw. It was impossible tOdo anything for the men who were washed from the boom, and the steamer set out for Runcorn, young Holden being treated by the men with the utmost kindness. He was landed at the Duke's Pier at Runcorn, and pro- • ceeded to .Penketh. The action of the crew of the Bridgewater was spoken of in terms of great 4ad- miration by the seamen, who know something of the perils of the river during a storm. Whilst Hol- den was waiting on the Widnes railway platform for a train his mother arrived from Penketh with clean clothing for her husband and sons, and the meeting of mother and son was of a most heartrend- ing description. The deceased man Holden leaves a - widow and large family, one a baby seven months old. Great Sympathy is manifested in Penketh for Mrs. Holden and her family. During the morning the flat Sarah Ann, belonging to Mr. William Cooper, of Widnes, capsized between Runcorn and Weston Point. The crew, consisting of John Mercer, James-street, Widnes; Jas. Moss, also living at Widnes, and another man named Swindells, were placed in imminent psril. With. great difficulty they got into the small boat and pulled to shore, nttrrowly escaping with their lives. Shortly afterwards the flat Thomas, belonging to Mr. Best, of Liverpool, manned by Abraham Houghton and his son Emmanuel, collided with the wreck 9f the Sarah Ann, and almost immediately sank. The two men`saved themselves by pulling to the shore in the small boat.

---.SO-ine-thi:illiTig-Tcen-e-s--Were witnessed at Elles- mere Port, Cheshire. During the height Of the gale on Thursday the two-mast flat ,W Hero, belonging to Messrs. Hill and Grundy, St. lens, was seen f,o be in great distress. The crew', four in number, got in- to a small boat, which was at once driven by wind and tide on to Stanlow Rocks, where they were as- sisted to land in a pitiable state. They were drenched to the skin and starved with cold. They were taken to Ellesmere Port, where they were most hospitably entertained. Three of the crew of the Dan, belonging to the same proprietors, were drowned. A steam flat was disabled in mid-chan- nel, having lost her propellor, and she had to re- main on the banks all day. At Widnes the heavy rainfall caused the works of the Widnes Foundry Company ;to be flooded to such an extent that a number of the men were un- able to continue their labours. The low-lying lands around Penketh and Ditton were covered with water. At the works of -Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. a pane of glass was dislodged from its frame- work, and alighted upon the head of a man named Robert Evans, who was in the act of getting his dinner. He sustained a scalp wound that penetrated to the bone, and was accompanied by extensive hemorrhage. He was taken to his home at 31, Prince's-street, phere the wound was stitched up by Dr. Hutchinson. ' The schoner Julia, of Runcorn, has been wrecked off Castletown, Isle of Man. All the crew were saved.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The Burmah business looks bad. When we have spent a few millions of money, and butchered some thousands of the natives, we shall perhaps begin to think that the annexa- tion of the country on the part of the Tory Government wasn't a very good thing after all.

In connection with the Conference of the Liberal Unionists in London on Monday, it was paraded as something significant that n 0 less than thirty noblemen had sent letters on the question. It is significant ; when it be- comes a question of Peers versus People, it is not difficult to say which, in the end, Will have to knock under.

The Liberal Unionists are disposed to make much of the no-rent movement in some parts of Ireland. But what if certain Nation- alists do break the law? Are the Liberals to be held responsible for that? Suppose a Liberal Unionist is brought before the magis- trates for being drunk and disorderly? Shall we argue from that that Liberal Unionists are a drunken and disorderly party?

Poor Pat He has a hard time of it. If he suffers silently, the Government say there is no need to interfere, and that legislation is unnecessary. If he resists what he believes to be evil, the Tories and the Liberal Unionists denounce him as an Anarchist who is not fit to be trusted—who must, rather, be schooled by twenty years of resolute govern- ment. But he may take courage; he hal Ireland, Scotland, and Wales on his side and England will be with him by-and-by.

The Spiritualists of Warrington seem to have entered upon a revival mission. They are a promising sect; but the objection that the sceptics take is that there is, as yet, more of promise than performance. When " Glen- dower " said—" I can call spirits from the vasty deep," " Hotspur " promptly replied— And so can I, or so can any MRII, But will they come when you do call for them? But will they come? Ay, there s the rub.

The Cunard Company, having lost the mail contract, are letting it be seen that they do not care to be at the beck and call of the Postal Authorities. It was a bold thing on the part of the captain of the Umbria to refuse the three mail bags which were being thrust upon him on Saturday last; but whe- ther it will prove to be a wise one is a point which must be left to the law courts.

-- The Tories of Warrington had obviously a poor case for appeal in the matter of the votes of the twenty soldiers quartered at Or- ford Barracks, Mr. Pierpoint, it may be presumed, made the best of it; but what that best was worth may be imagined when it is stated that the Judges didn't as much as call for the defence; they dismissed the appeal with costs. It is to be hoped the Conserva- tives like the result the Liberals do.

Sir A. I-3. Walker 1,3 a princely giver. He did a great thing for Liverpool when he pre- sented the City with an Art Gallery, and now he has intimated that he will furnish the University College of Liverpool with a labora tory for engineering, which, it seems, is very much needed. Will somebody whisper to him that Warrington has some little claim on his attention; that there is a Free Library which is not free; ang that, since his thoughts turn to things eduzational, there is a rare oppor- tunity of distinguishing himself during the Jubilee year.

The Liberals of the Northwich Division showed themselves to be thoroughly in earn- est at the Conference held at Runcorn on Monday. They not only accepted the pro- gramme of reform laid down at Leeds, but they enlarged it. They added three stout planks to the platform (I) the Disestablish- ment and Disendowment of the Church in Wales, (2) reform of the municipal govern- ment of the Metropolis, and (3) .rm of the House of Lords.

Lord Ripon well deserves the splendid re- ception that was accorded him at the evening meeting. It is no new thing for him to make a stand on behalf of an oppressed people. The nobleman who incurred the odium of the classes for daring to fight the battle of the masses in India is not likely to shrink when the question is one of justice to Ireland. His speech is such a one as might have been ex- pected from him—calm, well-reasoned, and statesman-like. He puts a very searching question to the Liberal Unionists. He wants to know, and other people want to know, " if their Liberalism for the future is to consist in sitting upon one side of the House.and voting upon the other ?"

What next, and next? The tithe agitators are at our very doors. The farmers have been holding a meeting at Burtonwood, and have resolved to ask the Rector, who is their tax- master, to forego zo per cent of the tithe. They have the hardihood to urge that, as they do the work and he takes the money, they have a right to live as well as he. That is where they are mistaken : they ought to starve in order that the landlord and parson may wax fat. And, then, how can a parson grow fat ol) less than £1,600 a year? Away with you, you foolish farmers. Why not, if you are hard pressed, eat grass like Nebu- chadnezzar? There is plenty of it.

Bingham, Haghem. Woods, F. Wright, and Morris. WARRINGTON HO/MITI Y. WIGAN ROYBR3 (IST TRAMS.) —The return match between these clubs'was played on Saturday last at Warrington. Lawless for the home team kicked off at 3-15, and no return being made play was con- fined to the visitors' quarters. Forster got over the line, but the ball was ruled beck. The game now became very fast, and in the end Wigan managed to score from a good dribble by their forwards, the kick at goal being a failure. On tbe change of ends Warrington had very hard lines in not storing. and on one occasion Doniels got over, but the ball was ruled back. The Hornets eantinned to have the best Of the game until Pritchard received a neat pass and drepped a splendid goal. Time be. ein shortly afterwards called leaving the Hornets victors of a'hard and fast game by 1 goal 5 minors to 1 try 3 minors. WARRINGTON 1" WIGAN "A " TRAMS. This match was played at Wigan on Saturday. Tbe home team were strong favourites., but the visitors added another victory to their long list. Simra kicked off for Wigen at 3-20, and Nevins failing to return, a scrimmage was formed in the visitors' qttarters, bat on the ball becoming looee Nevins punted to Crompton, who kicked into touch in the centre of the field. The Warringtonians were not to be denied, and after much loose play in the Wiesen querters Unsworth and Ashurst took the leather over the home line, the latter player gaining atry, which he by a good kick converted into a splen- did goal. Crompton kicked off, Unsworth returning. Im- mediately afterwards the Wigan forwards, headed by Ho- gan and Simms, rushed the bell over the Warrington line, Hewitt having to save by touching down. a singular rule of royal etiquette. It is geod form for the Queen to address one re- mark at least to each new guest, and here comes the test of the efficacy of Sir Henry Ponsonby's coaching. It is rather trying for a , novice, as, while the Queen speaks, everyone else is silent, so that your reply is heard by the whole din- ner table. It is not etiquette to address a remark directly to. the Queen. If you have a subject in which you think she may be interested you open it to your neighbour, and then Her Majesty may ask you directly about it. Every one has heard how the Queen met Carlyle at Dean Stanley's, and being interested on some point connected with German history, asked his opinion upon it. The old sage of Chelsea replied that as the subject was a large one, and not capable of being talked out in a couple of moments, it would be as well if Tier Majesty was seated. Queen Victoria had never before been asked to take a chair. She was perfectly delighted with the proposal, with the novelty of it, with the manner of it, and with Carlyle himself. I forgot to mention that at a royal dinner I have described, the guests do not remain for wine. When the Queen rises, her guests follow her, and the banquet is over.

It is curious to see the effect of this season on the London shopkeeper. All the shopkeepers who have not bough; a bankrupt's stock, seem to be at the eve of bankruptcy themselves. Desperate bargains are announced, and everything except postage stamps may be had at half price. Still town looks prosper- ous and happy. The glass has gone up, and during the firist few days of the week we have had lots of sunshine. The theatres are crammed. In fact, for the last few years the precedent has broadened of .practically celebrating Christ- mas towards the beginning instead of to- wards the end of December. Turkeys, plum pud- ding, roast beef, boxing day, and the pantomime are, of course, constant to the Church festival. But London, that is full of holiday folks now, the shops that in the teeth of universal bankruptcy are doing a roaring trade, and the theatres that have their novelties well launched—all admit that this is their busy season. This day fortnight London will be comatose, and, if not empty, emptying. We anti- cipate everything. The Christmas numbers are bought and read and thrown away before Christ- mas week is entered on, and the interest in the Christmas sirloin is ante-dated so as to be concen- trated as the prize bullock in the show. I am very glad to hear that some remonstrance is to be made to the authorities on the issue of a com- paratively recent regulation. Perlups the subje ct seems a slight one. It is the departure of troops for foreign service silently from their ports of embarka- tion. In old times, and in quite recent ones too. it was if to some a sad, yet to all a stirring and impressive sight to see a troopship atart for India. The decks were crowded with the red coats, the bands struck up "The girl I left behind me," or other appropriate melodies, and the cheers were loud and ringing. This emotion and excitement were obviously spon- taneous. The men certainly were not ordered to cheer. But now they are ordered not to cheer.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB:
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB:

At the conclusion of the match between Warring- ton and Wigan, on Saturday, the visitors were en- tertained to a sumptuous repast at the Lion Hotel. Besides the two teams, several influential gentle- men were present at the invitation of the Warring- ton Committee, amongst whom were Councillor Francomb (president of the club), Mr. Cronshaw (president of the Wigan club), Captain Reynolds, Messrs.Knowle-s (Wigan),Parry and Wilcox (secretary and treasurer of the Union), Mr. T. Morris, Mr. Fleming, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Mr. Gray, Mr. Warren and Mr. Naylor (two secretaries), and Mr. Pember, ton and Mr. Gerard (two treasurers). After the cloth had been removed the usual loyal toasts were drunk. Then came the toast of " The Visitor," res- ' ponded to by Mr. Knowles, who said he was glad to have witnessed such a good game, and to se the good feeling which prevailed between the two clubs.—" The success of the West Lan- cashire and Border Towns Rugby Union" was proposed by Mr. Craw}, in an able man- ner.—Mr. CRONSHAW, on rising to respond, was received with cheers. He spoke at some length on the merits of the two teams, and said that the three W's—Warrington, Widnes, and Wigan—would in time make themselves heard on the County Corn- mittee.—Mr. PARRY and Mr. WiLcox also made a few well-chosen remarks about the doings of the Union.—Captain RIVYNOLDS next proceeded with the toast of the evening "The health of Mr. Taylor, builder of the new stand.* He praised Mr. Taylor for the excellent manner in which he had fulfilled his task, and for doing it in less time than had been allowed him by the Committee.—Mr. TAYLOR, in re- sponse, said that his principle was that anything that was worth doing was worth doing well, and he had carried this out in regard to the stand, and hoped the Club and its supporters would derive much benefit therefrom.— Mr. BAR:T.IIIS was next called upon to ay a few words, and expressed his regret that an old and familiar face was, on this momentous occassion, absent, namely, Mr 11. Ashton, who, he was sorry to say, was suffering from a severe attack of inflam- mation.—Mr. ANDARTON proposed "The health of the Warrington President," and thailked him for occupying the chair.—Mr. Councillor FRA,Ncoun, in, replying, said he was always happy to be amongst the footballers, and he had every reason to be prowa of his team.—Messrs. Dillon, Anderton, and others enlivened the proceedings by singing in a praiseworthy manner. The Wigan party having to depart at nine o'clock,:a very enjoyable meeting was brought to & close.
THE MIT,TTARY FRANCHTSF,. CONSERVATITH APPEAL DISMISSED.

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Saturday, be- fore the Chief Justice, Baron Pollock, and Mr. Jus- tice Smith, the case Spittal T. Brook was heard. This was an appeal by twenty non-commissioned officers, who reside with their wives and families at Orford Barracks, Warrington, having separate rooms allotted to them by the military authorities, such rooms constituting dwelling-houses. The rooms were furnished by appellants, and were as- signed by the quarter-master, and could be changed by him. The rooms had been retained by appel- lants during the qualifying year, but they had been compulsorily absent on duty at Altcar for 27 days, during the qualifying year. While, however, they were absent on duty, their names were retained on the strength of the Warrington Regimental Depot, and the rooms continued to be occupied by their furniture and families. It was not denied that the quarter-master could resume possession of the rooms at any time and allot the appellants to other rooms. one of the appellants except Jas. Logan, a warrant officer, could, while compulsorily absent on duty at Altcar or elsewhere, return to personal inhabitancy of his rooms without a written-permis- sion or pass signed by the colonel or commanding officer prescribing the number of hours and the pur- pose for which permission was granted, as well as the hours between which it could be used. Reasonable leave was, however, granted to persons in the position of the appellants as of course, and the majority of the appellants had availed them- selves of the privilege and eturned to Warrington for some days during the period of absence. Logan's permission was verbal. The objection was that the appellants had not occupied the premises the qualifying year, and the revising barrister dis- allowed the votes.

Mr. Pierpoint appeared for the appellants, and Mr. R Henn Collins, Q.C., and Mr. J. 11. Williams for the respondents. Mr. Pierpoint argued that the residence was suf- ficient, and that the barrister was wrong. His decision, no doubt, was founded on the decision last year in the case of "Ford Y. Barnes" (16 Queen's Bench Division reports, 168), which is certainly prima !curie in point. —Lord Coleridge: Is it not en- tirely so? It is submitted that it is distinguish- able.—Lord Coleridge: Here there was a compulsory absence for 27 days. We must overrule that case to decide this differently. In that case the court said it was doubtful whether the man could have re- turned to•his residence.—Lord Coleridge: The cases are in substance the same. His inhabitancy was compulsorily broken by the rules of the service which gave him the qualification. Not the rules of the service ?—Lord Coleridge: Yes; he was absent under the rules of the service. There is no arguable distinction between this and the other case.
Mr. Henn-Collins, Q.C., on the other side, was not called upon. Lord Coleridge: The appeal must be dismissed, with costs.

TETE GOVERNMENT AND TRH CUNARD COMPANY.—In the Court of Queen's Bench, on Thursday, the Attorney- General applied on behalf of the Crown for an , injunction to restrain the Cunard Steamship Company from refusing to carry the mails for America. Sir Charles Russell at once applied for an adjournment of the case, on the ground that the information was only served in Liverpool on Tues- day morning last. He suggested next Tuesday for the hearing. It was agreed that the application should stand over till that day, subject to the convenience of all parties. div.head: RUNCORN RIFLE VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: RUNCORN RIFLE VOLUNTEERS.

DISIRIBU HON OF PRIZES. The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connec- with the I, and G (Rencorn) companies of the 2nd Cheshire Volunteers was held in the Runcorn Public Hall on Wednesday evening. A fashioneble, if not a very numerous company assetnialed, and were rewarded by having the plea- sure of listening to a musical performa.ece of exceptional merit. The exceeding wildness of the weather and other at- tractions militated against the atteudance to a great extent. The artistes were :—Soprano, Louie Richardson, of the Manchester and Liverpool concerts ; contralto, Miss Annie Itichardeon, of Liverpool Philharmonic concerts ; tenor, Mr. Webeter Williams, late of the Abbey Westminster; beseo profandi, Mr. John Thompsoc, of Chester ; buffo vocalist, Mr. J. H. Greenwood, of Manchester ; solo pinanoforte, Miss Bertha Henkiuson. Miss Annie Xcherdeon sang " Never again" and "Masks and faces " with much taste and expressien, and Miss Louie Richardson, who under the circumstance that she was suffering from a severe cold, was very successful in her rendition of " When the heart is voting "and "Tell me my heart." Mr. Williams, who is a tenor of great purity of tone and power, gave a most artistic and enjoyable interpretation of "The sailor's grave " and "Once again." In respoose to an enthusiastic recall he favouied the audience with a capital rendering of "Tom Bowling." Mr. J. H. Greenwood contributed two clever character sketches, and had to respond to an encore on each occasion. Mr. John Thompson sang with good effect "The diver and "Big Ben,' songs to which his wide range of voice was well suited. Miss Hankinson,.a musical genius, performed with a skill that secured her an enthusi- astic recall, a couple of solos on the pianoforte. The 'ailed of the corps wes responsible for two selections, which were given with their accustomed ability. During an interval in the programme th 3 prizes were dis- tributed by Mrs. McKinstry, the wife of the newly ap- pointed adjutant, who was introduced by Colonel Ashton. In doing so Colonel Ashton made a speech on the progress of the volunteer movement. Ia 1860, 150,000 volunteers were enrolled, of which 873 per cent were efficient. In 1885 there were 225,000 volunteers, and the percentage of efficients was 97.12. In 1875 their battalion numbered 521; in 1880 there were 623, and at the present time their num- bers totalled to 841—(applause)--and of this 839 were efficient, so that they would observe that there were only two non-efficients throughout the battalion. (Applause.) Coming to the Runcorn companies, that detachment was in 1876 composed of one company, numbering a little over 70 men. In 1880 it numbered 104, and at the present time the detachment was composed of two companies and numbered 191. (Applause.) Alluding to the prize list, Colonel Ash- ton complimented the Runcorn companies on their effici- ency and upon their skill in firing, special mention being made of Sergeant Harvey. Mrs. McKinstry then distributed the prizes as printed below. . On the proposition of Captain Hazlehurst, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. McKinstry, and the adjutant suitably responded on her behalf. however, who was standing offside, collared Hewitt with the ball in hes possession, and the latter, after grounding the ball, lost it, and Wigan claimed a try, which the referee granted. Crompton then kicked a good goal. Antrobus was afterwards conspicuous by a good run and pass to Handles, who was brought down by Clarke. Mitchinson now gave France a pass, this player putting in a good run, only being brought down by Hewitt a few yards from the line. When half-time was called, the score stood—War- Warrington 1 goal, to Wigan 1 goal and 1 minor. Whittle recornmenoed, and a 'poor rater' being made. France had to kick into touch. From the throw oat the home forwards took the ball to the visitors' line, Antrobua relieving by panting it into touch. The Wigan front rank now rushed the ball over the line, but Hewitt touched down. For a considerable time the Wigan lines were in danger, but France removed the pressure by punting to Nevin, who obtained a free kick but nothing came of it. Uosworth and Whittle were in- strumental in working the ball to the borne 25, where Mather picked up and gained the best try of the day, but Ashurst failed to repeat his previous performance in the goal kicking line. Thit brought about no side, Warrington being declared winners by 1 goal and 1 try to Wigan 1 goal and 3 minors. The Warrington forwards played a splendid game, their combination being far superior to that of the previous week. The backs played a good game all round. For Wigan. Crompton, France, and Baldwin behind, and Hogan, simm, and Swift forward, were most conepiceous. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Hewitt; half backs, Whittle (captain) and Antrobus : three-quarter backs, Handles, Unswortb, and Mather; forwards, Molyneax, Tel- ford, Nevins, Adamson, Jones, Eves, Hackett, Ashurst, and Holland. Wigan: Fall back, Crompton; half backs, Mit- chinson and Baldwin; three-quarter backs, France, Bootle, and Clarke; forwards, Simm (captain),-Yates, Grime, Swift, Hogan, Iforsefield, Ellison. Finch, and Smith. WARRINGTON T. WIGAN. There was an unusaally large gathering on the ground off Wilderspool-causeway, Warrington, on Saterday.to witness the contest between Warrington and Wigan first teams. The occasion was also marked by the formal opening of the new grand stand, by the President of the Warrington Foot- ball Club. Councillor Frencomb, J.P. The grand stand is large, shapely, and very strong, and although it is capable of accommodating a great number of spectators, it was quite full, amongst those present being Colonel Thackwell, under the patronage of whom, and ether officers of the Bth and 40th Regimental District, the match was played. On the field altogether there were about 7,000 spectators. The Warrington team were the first to appear on the field, and immediately their opponents, who were a likely-looking set, came on, play was begun. Amongst the forwards Warring- ton were short of Ashton (captain), through illness, and , Wigan wanted the services of Whittle. Wigan won the spin up, and elected to defend the town i goal, with a sliglq wind in their favour. Frank Turner,, therefore, kicked off, and Massey, following well up, pre- vented a return. The Warrington forwards, working well together, confined play inside the visitors' territory. Barnes had a free kick, Turner (Fair) taking the place, which did not result in anything. Barnes afterwards took a flying kick, the ball catching Aspinall, be gained a few yards, tat was well stopped by the elder Turner. Again scrimmages took place, and Hunter popped the ball into the hands of Samuels, who ran along touch finely, but was cleverly checked by Appleton when a try seemed almost a certainty. The Warrington forwards, headed by Rigby and Davies, however, removed, and Hunter put in a nice pass to Ander- ton, the latter player soon after nicely collaring Massey with the ball in the home 25. Speakman, however, picked up and kicked to touch. The Warrington forwards, aided by Gilbert, again made a dash, but were checked by Hunter, and the Wiganers, chief amongst whom were noticed Bray- shay and Kay, again took play to the home 25. Hunter new made a good pass to Slevin, but Barnes was on the alert, and intercepted it, gaining a good lot of ground by so doing. Semnals again tried to get in a long run, but was made to kiss mother earth by a good collar. ailbert re- ceived the oval from a long throw out, and kicked up the fiel 1, then followed up quickly, but not fast enough to prevent Anderton, sen., returning. Barnes now stopped a dangerous rush of the visitors' forwards, and soon after intercepted a pass intended for Slevin, and Gilbert, following up, collaree the full back with the ball, which put the Wiganers on the defensive. The little centre got hold, and essayed to drop at goal, a minor resulting for the home team. Slevin kicked off, Frank Turner returning, and Rigby caused a scrimmage to be formed by taking hold of the ball off-side. Grundy now took the oval after Turner had made a rush, and Harris fol- lowing up with the rest at his keels, the home goal line seemed in danger; but Massey promptly kicked to touch. From the line out a scrimmage was formed, S. Kaye coming through to be brought down by Appleton on the line. The home forwards by sheer hard work removing play to the 25, Davies, Rigby, and Dillon working like horses. Ander- ton next received a pass from Hunter, but Appleton was on the look out and pushed him into touch. He threw out quickly, but the home forwards quickly stopped any further progress. Barnes again intercepted a pass for Anderton, and Jolley, he, and Gilbert following took the oval to the Wigan quarters. Povey, Dillon, and Davies here showed up, a dead ball being the result of their united play. The Wigan full back had now to retire, Wardle taking his place, and Slevin kicked off, Appleton returning. Barnes now put in a pretty pass to Jolley, who took the ball to the line. The half-back next passed Barnes, who kicked, and the ball going wide Jolley raced up and grounded the oval over the line. The place was a difficult °He, and Speakman failed to improve matters. A piece of good pity was next witnessed by Gilbert, which brought about half time. On the ball being re-started, Barnes rgturned, Gilbert and Jolley being very soon conspicuous by good drib- bling and tackling. Massey now kicked hard, which brought about another minor. From the kick out Brayshay followed well up, Fair Turner and Jolley being at a loss which of them to rake the ball, play settling down for some time in neutral quarters. Dillon, however, re- moved hostilities to the Wigan quarters, where Littlewood got hold and made a splendid dash ever the line, wring the second try for the home team. Frank Turner was this time entrusted with the place, and amidst great cheering, kicked a beautiful goal from a very difficult position. Ap- pleton returned the kick off, Anderton putting in a kick in f return, only to fall into the hands of Fair Turner, who punted, and Massey following well up, gained ground. Jolley next tackled Anderton in a splendid manner, War- rington penning the visitors in their own 25. W. PoveY now showed up very prominently, coming through in grand style. The Wigan forwards, headed by Brayshaw, 4 ay. and Dempsey, now strove hard to get away, but were checked by Speakman. Anderton, however, removed dan- ger by a nice run, from a pass by Hunter. Speakman next next got hold and seemed likely to score, but preferred to drop at goal, a minor resulting. Slevin after the kick out got in a nice run, but was checked by Barnes, who replied with a nice dodgy run. Gilbert put in a good pass to Barnes, who repassed to Massey, a minor being the result. Darkness now set in, and it was impassible to single out in- dividual work; suffice to say that the home team had the best of it, and after a very pleasant and well-coateated game of 70 minutes, the cup-holders ran out winners by one goal , one try, and five minors to nothieg. - The game on the wh de was a splendid exhibition of foot- ball, scientific play and good passing being the order of the day. Both teams seemed desirous of making the game as open as possible, this doing away with the rough work cone nected with packed scrimmages, the few packed there were the home team had the best of them. Both teams played finely on the loose, and it was pleasing to witness the good feeling which prevailed between the two teams. Appleton at full back again proved a valuable acquisition in the ranks of the first team, kicking and tackling with a cool head and good judgment, two points which are necessary in the qualification of a full back. It must not be omitted that he saved what seemed to be two certain tries, one by Samuels and the other by Anderton, tackling the first-named in grand style, and pushing the latter into touch. Barnes, the centre three-quarter, played an excellent game, outplaying his opponent and several times taking his passes. If he would feed his wing men a little more he would himself have more ehances of displaying his goal-kicking abilities, and would stand second to nano in the county. Jolley did good service in the tackling department, and also ran well. Massey again played well on the defence. In the first half, how- ever, he seemed rather careless, but made up for it in the second by his nice runs and kicks. Speakman was particu- larly noticeable for his good defensive game, especially, when Warrir.igton were hotly pressed not allowing the ball to come past him; but Gilbert shone most in this position, excelling; in all the good points to be found in a half-back. The for- wards one and all played with a determination to win, Lit- tlewood's run belng especially worthy of notice. Davies, Dillon, Rigby, and Povey also took a very prominent part in the tusle. Pair Turner did not quite show his true form, bat suffering as he did from a severe cold, be played sur- prisingly. Anderton, the Wigan full back, played well until he was hart, his place being filled by Wardle, who did not show up as well as his predecessor. Slevin had very little to do. Anderton was spoiled by Barnes, bat still managed to get in some of his. noted strong runs. Samuels nut in a lot of useful work, his runs being the longest of the day, as on account of his speed it wanted a good runner to bring him down. The two half-backs were outplayed by their opponents, hut still played in a plucky and praiseworthy manner. The forwards played a good combined game, Brayshay and S. Kay showing up as good examples to their comrades. Teams :—Wigan : Back, Anderton, senior ; three-quarter backs, Slevin (captain), J Andertcn, J C Samuels ; half- backs, J Aepinall, J Hunter; forwards, J Brayshay, W At- kinson, JEI Lowe, S Kay, W Wells, Dempsey. Grandy, Wardle, Harris. Umpire, leir Leyland. Warrington; Back, Appleton; three-quarter beck, Jolley, Barnes, Massey ; half- backs. Gilbert (captain), Speakman ; forwards, Fair Turner, F Turner, Povey, Littlewood, Hayes, Dillon, Rigby, and Hough. Umpire, Mr Barnes. Referee, Mr Lord, Broughton Rangers. -

NOTES BY TETE WAY. The Warrington Committee deserve every praise for the manner in which they turn out their teams, last week the cup holders appearing with new jerseys, which are a lot ahead of anything we have seen on ;be homa ground, being narrow primrose and blue stripes, with turn down collar attached. After supplying the first team last week, it is rumoured that the "A" team are to be treated in the same manner to-day. It was pleasing to see the friendly game which was played -on Saturday between Warrington and Wigan, and this was, no doubt, owing to a great extent, to the good generalship of the two captaina, and to the prompt decisions of the re- feree, Mr. Lord. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TIMISDAT. The Irish crisis has come upon the Government like a thunder clap. Its difficulties are two-fold. It cannot advance and it cannot recede. The policy of sending Mr. W. H. Smith with a reporter's noto-book and a return ticket ended so disastrously last year that it has not been repeated, and it is hard for a Cabinet to put its foot down when the process is found to leave it without a leg to stand on. The Government are, moreover, in one terrible difficulty. There are not one or two, but seyeral of the Nationalists in their employ in Dublin Castle, and these "ehiels" take notes and print them. I hear the only gleam of hope the Cabinet has lies in 1 a quite unexpected direction. They must begin with their procedure measure before they can at- tempt anything in the nature of a Crimes Bill. Whatever they may say about sequence, they know- well that this is the only possible order. And their hope lies in this direction? If proclamations and prosecutions should succeed—the success is possible but certainly not probable—then the Crimes Bill will be unnecessary, but if they fail the failure will certainly be noted and emphasised by the Nation- alist party. Immunity will lead to defiance and things will get not merely bad,•but very bad. Mr. Parnell has always realised that the problem for him was to keep his lieutenants and his host under discipline. Irish politics rarely stand still. Lord Salisbury hopes they may get so bad that his co- ercion act should be a necessity. I hear repeated on all sides that the Home Seers. tary is tired of office and anxious to give it up- Every lawyer who wants to be a Cabinet Minister and does not care to be Lord Chancellor aspires to preside at the Home Office. It was the pet arebi- tion of Sir Henry James, and here is Mr. Matthews already keen to vacate the post. Two problems would then come before the Cabinet. Who would they appoint as Home Secretary, and what would they do with the new minister's predecessor? Would hi accept a puisne judgeship? Henry Matthews never was much of a lawyer. He is one of the few men yet remaining at the bar who hays the natural gift of eloquence. He speaks like an orator, so did the late Sir John Karstake, so does Mr. David Plunket. But none of the three was a lawyer. Here is one rumour that has got about. Lord Blackburne is tired of being a law lord. His 'le is rather monotonous. He drives down in a

handsom from Princes-gate to Westminster, smoking all the way—no judge on the bench has ever con- sumed so much tobacco—and takes his seat amongst the law lords and cracks legal cruxes (cruces) all day, then turns in to the Atheneum where he meets the puisne judges whom he remembered at the bar, and then makes way home to his bachelor house at Princes Gate. He never goes to a theatre, or a con- cert, or a picture gallery. He is unquestionably the greatest lawyer now living. He is an old bachelor who cares for nothing but law—except tobacco. I hear it is proposed to fill up his vacancy by appoint- ing Sir James Stephen, and to fill Sir James' va- cancy.by appointing Mr. Matthews a puisne in his place. There is great speculation about Lord Tennyson 's new volume, which will be published in a few days by Macmillan. No poet has so often changed his publisher. He began with Moxen in days when every poet found:it prudent to deal with this most eclectic of book issuers. Then he went to Strahan for a short time ; then he changed again, and took up with Kegan Paul, and now at last he takes al) with Macmillan. The volume will contain a second part of "Locksley Hall," said; I hear, not to be at all so happy in inspiration as the first. We have not done yet with the Collins and Gosse controversy. Mr. Collins and Mr. Swinburne were fast friends once. The poet gave his admirer a few years ago the original MS. of the most beautiful of his recent lyrics. The poet of " Atanta in Calydon "has no stauncher admirer than the " Quarterly Reviewer." But poets are " kittle cattle' to deal with. Mr. Col- lins unfortunately said that Mr. Swinburne was a great poet but a poor prose writer, and all ,Par- nassus is up in arms. Mr. Swinburne is hard at work on a pamphlet which is to answer that review in the "Quarterly." The pamphlet may be a great success, but if it should prove so, it will be the first prose success the poet will have scored. Except the late Lord St. Leonards—l mean the first Lord St. Leonards—l don't know any eminent writer with so bad a prose style. We are likely to be flooded with fasting men. Either the secret of Succi's marvellous liquor has transpired, or else there are several liquors which have the same power, or else the whole thing is imposture. It must be one of the three. A French- man has now started in. London on a career of famine. He has taken up his quarters in a pleasant little West End hotel in Jermyn-street. which Rubinstein and JoaChim—very different guests— have been wont to patronise. I am told great care has been taken to secure him a room as far as pos- sible from the kitchen. - He finds that when he is fasting it is most irritating to endure the smell of roast beef. One can not but sympathise with this touch of nature. He has now entered on the ninth day of his fast., which is to be continued for 30 days. He is a Frenchman—Celts seem to have a facility for this kind of fasting—but I wonder whether, if more of this starvation craze should spread, the Lord Chamberlain might not intervene. Still, Englishmen as a rule are not given to starvation. The Colin Campbell case still drags on, and seems likely to run into another week. Lady Colin has managed to keep her portraits out of the market. Everyone is surprised to find that they are not in the shop windows. Whatever else may be said or thought of her, at least she never posed as a Profes- sional Beauty. She had all the opportunities for publicity, but publicity of this kind she does not seem to have cared about. I remember her being at a certain private view at the Grosvenor, where Mary Anderson, Ellen Terry, Mrs. Langtry, and Mrs. Bernard-Beere were all present, and present, so to speak, several times. Lady Colin had a look of dis- tinction an a supurb haughtiness which no.ne of the others could assume. Her portraits, if they could be got, would now be worth a good deal. How amusing, and yet how distressing, it must have been for Lord Walter Campbell to find his own wife'a portrait hawked about in the London streets as that of the alleged adulteress. And there is not the smallest resemblance between the two ladies. When the Duke got into the witness box there was a little buzz in the court. Everyone noticed how old he looked, and how heavily the yearS that am not Time's had weighed him down. He has lost that dignity and self-assertion which used to be- long to him. He seemed tired and anxious, and seated himself soon after he got into the box with- out asking the Judge's leave. Sir -Charles Butt looked up for a moment, but said nothing. • Sir Henry Ponsonby's functions at Court are onerous and amusing. It is painful to think what might happen if he were suddenly taken ill and unable to discharge them. Many guests have the honour of dining at Windsor who on that occasion have the experience of being seated for the first time in a room with Her Majesty. Their prepara- tion for this ordeal is entrusted always to Sir ; Henry. He receives the novices on arrival at the Castle, and has a little interview with each, during J which he explains to him the courtesies of the oc- casion. Then the guests are taken to their rooms, and afterwards are introduced to the Queen in her private drawing-room. The interview lasts for a few minute's, and then there are the morns in the Castle, the picture gallery, and the pleasure grounds to be inspected . until dinner time; for the arrival of guests is fixed for six o'clock, and the dinner hour tor nine. A quarter before that hour the gong, which has already sounded twice, sounds now for the last time, and the guests troop into the draw- ing-room. Ten minutes later the Queen enters, says a word tq each guest, and then leads the way down to dinner. And working one sees the workin of

div.head: GREAT FIRE AT WIDNES.
div.p: GREAT FIRE AT WIDNES.

The chemical works of Messrs. N. Matheson and Co., Widnes, were the scene of 'a most disastrous fire on Sunday morning. Nearly the whole of the buildings recently erected for the manufacture of soda by the ammonia process were destroyed, and the valuable engines and machinery with which they were filled were seriously damaged. The en- gines and machinery and other plant had been con- structed with the greatest care and secrecy, as the patent is a valuable one, and was expected to bring back to the town some of the trade absorbed by the Winnington Wolks of Messrs. Brunner and Mond. Operations were commenced about three weeks age to a third of the extent that Messrs. liathieson ulti- mately expected to carry on the manufacture of soda ash and carbonate of soda, and the fact that some months must elapse before the works will be in a similar position again constitutes a grave loss. The fire was discovered at five minutes past six by a watchman named Thomas Newton, who.observed flames issuing from the south side of the buildings. Mr. L. Kilcross, the yard malinger, who lives on the premises, was quickly aroused, and gathering; to- gether the eight or nine men who were on duty, connected a hose with one of the numerous hydrants in the works, and in a few minutes a stream of water was poured on the blueing building. The structures being principally of wood, having roofs covered with tarred felt, the flames spread with fearful rapidity, and when the fire engine and brigade arrived on the spot at seven o'clock the '" new works" were one mass of , flames. Under the command ot Mr. Superintendent Carr, the brigade, Which had obeyed the alarm with commendable despatch, worked with much judgment and energy. Although there was no lack of water, it was soon discovered to be impossible to , quench the flames that were consuming the en- gine-house, the fitting shop, and the furnace shed, and the men successfully set about to save the boiler shed from the devouring element. The mem- bers of the brigade were often placed in positions of imminent peril through the falling of massive beams and heavy pieces of machinery, but there was no shrinking from duty, and the admirable manner in which they laboured was the subject of favourable comment amongst the hundreds of spec- tators who had assembled in the vicinity. An ex- citing incident occurred about nine o'clock. Placed over a number of towers, at least 50 feet from the ground, was a large iron tank, weighing about 23 tons, and supported by huge beams. The supports were destroyed one by one, and at length the huge mass fell upon the machinery below with a tremendous crash. In its descent, however, it came in contact with one of the inner walls, and thus causing it to overturn and thus .causing it to alight with less velocity than it other- wise would have done. The fire was totally extin- guished at noon, but only the brick walls and iron towers and the boiler-house remained standing,. The loss is roughly estimated at between 230,000 and £40,000,i which is fortunately covered by in- surance.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly metting of this Board was held at the Whiston Workhouse on Thursday. Mr. William Tyrer presided, and there were also present the Rev. Thomas Chambers, Messrs. J. W. Wareing, C. B. Johnson, W. Mid- dlehurst, J. Whalley. Joseph Ellison, James Burchall, E. Svder, T. F. Hill, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk) Work- house Statistics: Mr. Hale reported that there 455 inmates this week, against 475 last week and 467 in the correspond- ing period of last year. Number of vagrants reli.ved 66, against 37 in the corresponding period of last Year.:—The Christmas Dinner: The Master asked if it was the inten- tion of the Guardians to give the usual Christmas dinner to tbe inmates.—The Rev. Thomas Chambers moved, and Mr. Wareing seconded, that the annual dinner of roast beef and plum pudding be given to the inmates on Christ- mas Day. The Clerk said the inmates were sup- plied with as much beef as they could eat. The ques- tion of beer had never been discussed by that Board, and he did not think it would be that day. The inmates had beer, but no excess had been noticed in the past, and he did not think there would be any. The resolution was Passed. Expenses of CorY'erenees: A letter was read from.the Secre- tary to the North-Western Poor Law Conference intimating that a levy of 25s would have to be made on each Union represented to meet the expenses. It was also suggested that au admission fee should be imposed on delegates enter- ing, and so meet the expenses in that way in future. The Clerx remarked that if they had to pay a levy they could pay, but he did not care about being taxed when be went to a conference. (Hear, hear.)—The Widnes Oeclical Officer : Dr. Cooper, medical officer for Widnes, asked the Guardians to accept Mr. Hutchinson as his substitute while he paid a visit to his son, who was ill in London.' The Clerk said that Dr. McClellan was recognised as Dr. Cooper's substi- tute by the Board, but if Dr. McClellan chose to make arrangements with Mr. Hutchinson they ironld not object, but they held him responsible.—The Milk Contract : Mr. Philip Lowcock, the milk contractor, asked to be allowed to deliver milk to the House only once a day during the winter, instead of twice as stated in the eontract.—Mr. Wareing said several practical Guardians were of opinion that as milk delivered in the evening would have cream on it in the morning, and that while some inmates would get all cream others would only get skimmed milk, it would be an injustice.—On the motion of Mr. Hill, secsnded by Mr. Ellison, it was decided to hold Mr. Lowcock to hie contract. The Contract for Supplies: The Clerk was instructed to advertise in the local papers for tenders for the supply of provisions, !sc.. for the Workhouse for the next six months. —The Distress in Prescot: The Clerk stated that Mr. -John- son and himself had attended the Central Poor Law Confer- ence in London on the previous day, and laid bsfore those present the views of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians. They urged that exceptional distress existed in Unions beyond the bounds of the metropolis, and that it was not only the duty of the Guardians to enquire into the cause of the distress but go further and suggest a remedy. The distress amongst the Prescot watch- makers was alluded to, but only incidentally. They wished to establish the principle that boards of guardians as boards of guardians ought to inquire into the cause of depression,

Mr. Gladstone replying to Mr. Ellis Lever, in reference to the metropolitan coal tax, says be agrees with Mr. Levers's condemnation of the tax, and states that if Lord B. Churchill holds to his position, the tax must be on its last legs. Tug ELEMORE COLLIERY DISASTER.—During Saturday the work of exploration was carried on without cessation, and in both seams which were blocked the exploring par- ties penetrated to the furthest extent of the workings. Fourteen bodies were recovered. A relief fund has been opened at the colliery, and the officers of the Darham and Northumberland Permanent Relief Fund have also been most active in distributing the allowances for deceased members. All the' bodies are now out of the Eleuaore Pit, except one. Eighteen victims of the explosion were on Monday interred at Easington. AyTEmETED MURDER AND SUICIDE.— At Wolverhamp- ton, on Saturday, Margaret Howard, 34, of Melbourne- street, was charged with attempting to commit suicide. On Friday evening prisoner was in the neighbourhood of a canal, when she was beard to say to a child about three years of age, who accompanied her, "This is the place, Maggie, where you and I are to end our days. lam in deep trouble, and cannot bear it any longer." Taking up the child, who began to scream, the prisoner advanced to- wards the canal, when she was stopped by a boatwoman, who took the child from her. The prisoner said that as the child was hers, she cauld do as she liked. She seemed very excited, and admitted afterwards that she had been in- dulging in drink. She was remanded. --- - A curious old lady wants to know if the "editorial sallies" she hears so much about are the sisters of the "printers' devils." A well-known Baptist minister tells the following story—" When in London a few weeks ago, I visited a fishmonger's, and asked the name of a peculiarly ugly fish that lay on tie counter. We call them Baptists, replied the dealer. 'Baptists!' I rejoined. Why Bap- tists!' Because,' he. answered, 'they go to the bad as soon as they come out of the water.'" The soene is a young ladies' day-school. " said ohe little girl to another, in triumph, "my mamma gives me a penny every morning for taking a spoonful of cod- liver oil !" "And what do you buy with the penny?" eagerly asked the second girl, in a tone not devoid of envy. "Oh," answered the first speaker, "I do not spend It at all ; mamma puts it away for me every day to buy more cod-liver oil with." We have all heard of a" squarson," though we may not all be able to say with whom the word originated; but who invented the word " squishop,"—i.o., a combi- nation of " squire " and " bishop" ? Canon Venables, writing to Notes and Queries, says the inventor was the late Bishop Wilberforce, just after he had succeeded to the estate of Layington. "Why, Wilberforce," said a .friend, "you've become a squarson." "No," was the reply—" a squishop." . SHOUT GUIDE POR Gint.s.—Do not "choose an oppo- site." You will be opposite enough in time. Take your mother's advice on the question of a husband, provided she took her mother's. Either put your foot down on his cigar before marriage or make up your mind to keep quiet about it afterward. Learn to sew and cook if you can, but above all things learn to keep still and look sweet when wild enough to blow the roof off. See and hear all the plays, operas, and concerts you can during the engagement; bad weather is very apt to interfere after marriage. They were old friends, and had been sweethearts in their younger days. There was silver in her hair and snow on his, and they sat and talked of old times when they were young. They did not say how many years ago the adventure happened. They did not speak of dates. It was "when we were young." Their first meeting, their first quarrel, their last kiss, their last quarrel were all gone over. Perhaps they both warmed a little over the recollections. At last he said: "Ay, Jennie, an' I hae na loved anybody since you. 1 has never forgotten you." " John, ' she said, with a little moistening of the eye- "You're just as big a lsear as ever—an' I believe ye, jist the same." Doctor: "Are your troubled with sleeplessness?" Patient: "Never." Doctor: "Do you ever have severe pains in the head or back ?" Patient: "None." Doctor: "Don't you often feel a disinclina- tion to work ?" Patient: "Well, yea" Doctor: "And a desire to lie abed late mornings ?" Patient: "Fre- quently." Doctor: "It is as I thought. Get this pre- scription put up at once, and take a teaspoonful every three hours in water. I'll call again to-morrow. Good day." THE DONKEY 2.1C1) TITH P/INO.—A donkey, haying heard the piano loudly played and the player greatly applauded, became jealous of his rights and set up a horrible bray. "You infernal beast, but what do you call that ?" demanded the master as he rushed forth. "Why, I intended it for music." "Then take that! and that! and that! for your ignorance !" shouted the man, as he fell upon the brayer with a hoe-handle. Moral: A. fox, who found the beaten donkey hanging his in- sulted head in the fields, asked for and received an ex- planation and then said: "My friend, there wasn't so much difference in the noise, but a Tory great difference in who made it." Hs VOTE.—" Here's a man around the corner I wish you'd talk to a little," said the friend of a candi- date as the two met on Michigan Avenue yesterday. "What ails him ?" "He says he won't vote at all at this election. Go and rouse him up and get his vote." The candidate palmed around the corner and found a stranger leaning up against the wall. He talked of the sacred Constitution—George Washington—Abraham Lincoln— free trade—protection, and so down, putting in a good half-hour before he stopped and inquired: "And you tell me you won't vote ?" "I don't expect to." "You don't? You, a man, and yet have no interest in keep- ing our politics pure by electing good men to office! You won't vote ?" "I guess not." "For heaven's sake, why r" "Because Pm a Canadian citizen and have no right to !"

PUBLIC BATHS IN WARRINGTON.

- Sir,—Kindlv allow me space for a word respecting tbe miserable accommodation provided by our Corporation for those vt .o deligut in the cleanly and healthful exercise of bathing. Aoyoue attnclitiw the present baths regularly would soon see the care of their being a failure, not that it should be held I.bat h bs should be self supporting. The attendart ce- ta;nly dnes all he car, t.) make the place toler- able, but at e bett it is very Oeficient. The swifflming baths shol.ld be tnucn larger and deeper, and the space and aocommodstion rourd. them should be greater. Rerorm in this respect would co ;i: a few pounds. but it would greatly increa,e the revenue, herar,,e many people would u,ei them then whn .411 not do co now. It would be rude to seem to concur in the general tamressioo that our Town Council is notoriouly low." It is, however, beyond all contradic- tion that there is great dilatoriness in giving this question the considera,ion it derervai—N on. e truly, HENRY RADNA"I4. Wilder.spool-road, 2nd December, 1886. THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION..

Sir,—lt is gratifying to hear that steps are being taken to make our Public Library into a "Free Lending Library," and, monover that men of both political parties can siek their differences of opinion and work together in a move- ment for the benefit of the inhabitants of this old town cf Warrington. I gather flan] our local newspapers that out of about £650 per annum required to maintain the Library and Mci.eum which are inseparable about £530 is now raised by a rate of one penny in the pound, the full amount allowed to be levied by the Libraries Act of Parliament. Although the ratenayers contribute three quarters of the income they are required to pay the subscription to be on a par with those outside the borough who do not pay the rate, but still they enjoy the benefits of a rate-aided institution. This, to Say the least, is unfair. In conclusion. I tender my thanks to the prime movers in the project, and hope the public will rally round and support them at the Town's Meeting to be convened by the Mayor. ONE ABOUT TOWN.

THE LATE BOATING FATALITY AT HOWLEY. Sir,—ln connection with this matter, I wish to bring one fact before the notice of those whom it may concern. I was one amongst hundreds who from day to day witnessed the praiseworthy efforts of those men in the boats grappling for the dead bodies. It was a dreary cold job and also risky. The man William Patten. in charge of on of the boats, found two of the bodies, and he with the rest of the men, spent four days in the search. For all their praiseworthy efforts on Wednesday last 7s, 6s, and 5s each was awarded them for their labours. It is on account of the dissatisfaction on the part of the men with the sum received, and their de- claring that they would not undertake the worK again, I am led to inquire on their behalf whether there is not some source from which they can get what the are clearly en- titled to—a good remuneration for their labcurs. If the authorities were to reward them I am sure no one would grumble. The quertion is very widely asked, who should be responsible for the expense and recovery of the bodies of those who may unfortanately get drowned, and you, sir, might be able to give an answer to it.—Yours truly. December 9th, 1886. S. DAVIES.

div.head: SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: SCHOOL OF ART.

Sir,—As everything connected with the School of A7l must have interest for most of your cultured readers, I think it is worth while to invite special attention to the ad- vertisement in your columns this week, which announces a free exhibition of the students' works on Tuesday and tbe two following days. Judging to some extent by past re- sults, I think the committee will feel confidence in antici- pating an exhibition considerably in advance of previous ones. I notice also there will be a number of students' works offered for sale, which means. I suppose, they will. be offered at reasonable prices and marked in plain figures. I think this is the first time students' works have been on sale, and it seems somewhat of a new departure. a depar- ture, however, if it proves successful in the matter of sales will be of service in a variety of ways. Primarily it will relieve the students of works that may have cost them much careful thought, but which, whether in a portfolio or framed and hung, must, in many cases, be only in the way, and the constant presence of them cannot have a very stimulating effect on the student's mind. Secondly, the study of even elementary art means something more than time; it includes money, and it is no small consideration to the studeats themselves, or to their parents, especially if two or three of a family have to be provided with the need- ful fees, drawing and painting materials, &c., required every quarter. Thirdly, I think that the sale of some of the se- lected works would do the school itself a world of good, and if some of our local connosseurs would spend a few pounds in this way on drawings and pictures which would do no discredit to their walls, they would give an inspiration to the students which at the present time is wanting. If the friends of the School of Art are unable to be present during the sale, lam sure a five or a ten pound note put into the bands of the master, or the indefatigable secretary, would be judiciously invested, and the full value obtained for the money. In conclusion, as one who has long felt in- terested in the progress of the School of Art,l am glad to be assured it was never in a healthier state or. doing better work than it is at the present time ; the conditions for study are superior to what they ever were before, and the teaching staff have the full confidence of the committee. A SUBSCRIBER.

div.head: SPIRITUALI6M V. CONJURING.
div.p: SPIRITUALI6M V. CONJURING.

Sir,—After reading the letter from "Justice " last Satyr- day, I was surprised to find that he considered my accept- ance of the challenge coupled with conditions that can be turned any way. Truth should have no fear, and I think a committee of gestlemen would see that., Justice " got justice. The persons he would allow to be present consists of only one uninterested kentleman—the Editor. Now one does not constitute a committee. I say let us have six more, " Justice "to select three, end myself three In cse of dispute between myself, " Justice " and the Medium, it must be left to the committee of six. If they fail to seitle it, then the Editor's decision to be final. • As regards the r mditions in applying the tests, I only want three : first, that I shall be allowed to wash the slate on which the answer is to be received, to the question which I shall have written on a piece of paper, so as to wash off any message which may have been written beforehand; second, that I shall be allowed to mark it to guard against substitution ; third, that I shall be allowed to seal the slate to guard against it being opened during the production of ,1 the phenomenon. As thes3 are the conditions under which I they say this phenomenon takes place, where is the ground of _objection.

Now let us look how " Justice " is putting it, and we shall see wheie the deception is. He mentions the word phenomena." Now what does this word mean. Why, a number of such things, and no one being specified. the Medium could ao whico ever he pleased. Let " Justice " strike out this word phenomena, and in its place put Spini • writing. We shall then be at the foundation of the challenge. As "Justice "does not care where this test takes place, I select Warrington. In regard to the Medium's expenses, in my last letter I stated if he wins his cau,,e, my £5 is taken for that pur- pose, but, if he thinks this is not sufficient, I propose we each add £lO to the sum al- ready stated, and which ever wins, picks it rp. Of course the original £5 goes towards the Warring- ton Infirmary. Now if "Justice " wins his cause, Caere will be sufficient to cover the Medium's expenses. I dont force this upon " Justice "; he has the first proposition to fall back upon; but I will pay half towards a room in which to test it. I leave the challenge open until the 17th inst., but if by that time the £5 deposit is not made, I shal

consider he has withdrawn his challenge. I shall feel jus- tified, too, in not replying to any more of his letters, and in denouncing Spiritualism as imposition, and Spirit Mediums as impostors. " Justice " said, If I know this to be a trick, it is my duty to expose it to the world. Well, I mean to do it. In answer to the question "is the magnet an intelligent force"? if he alludes to the magnet and the needle, I say it is not an intelligent force; if he alludes to animal mag- netism, it is an intelligent force, or how could they get in- telligent messages when they apply to a table? The irst- mentioned magnet is niarie by electricity, therefore only ar- tificial; animal magnetism is pure nature. If " Justice " thinks this explanation not sufficient; he may call at my house any time by appointment, and I will show him how to get electro-mpgnetism without the aid of Spirits. In re- ply to the question What of Professor Crooks"? in re- gard to the evidence of a number of well-known gentlemen, I refer him to my letter which anpeared in this paper on November 21th. lam yours, &g.. THOMAS ACTON. $9, Priestley-street, Warrington, Dec. etb, 1880.

Sir,—Allow me to confess at once to "Justice" that I am rightly served. All the opprobrium he could possibly heap upon my poor head, would be only a fitting chaetisement for the rashness I displayed in attempting so much as to iiisplay even the least little bit of curiosity respecting spirits and Spirit-land. Even now I am writing I scarcely know what te do or what to say. You see, " things are not what they seem," and "Justice" may be very unjust to me, by substituting for his own proper person some spiritual fiend to keep en torturing myself and your readers for an indefinite term, I trust to your kindness. Mr. Editor, to put the clown) on these spiritual gentry and so save us all from getting mixed up in what might turn ont a spiritual duel. I, like a whole host of your readers, attended the recent spiritual lecture, and was, as a matter of course, doomed to disappointment. We went to see the play of " Hamlet," and found all bat the hero himself. Well, we had to be content with what was placed before us, and in justice to Mr. Wallis, I must say he has learned his lesson. Such a jingle of words I never before heard. Talk of "playing with words," why, sir, your correspondent is not in it ; "words, words, words." Never before was anything heard like it. Had the "Trance Discourse" lasted much longer the Old Music Hall would have been transformed into a bedlam, for the listeners would most cer.ainly have been driven mad. Sir, I proposed to myself a little pleasure this week in roundly abusing Lord Randolph, and patting in a word in favour of Ireland, but it was net to be ; the Spirits d emed otherwise, and, consequently, the spiritnalised letter of "Justice" appears, and, against my wish, lam forced to notice the unsubstantial subject once more. "Justice" must bear, with a little patience, with the stu- pidness of men like myself who have not yet had the benefit of seeing behind the veil. If we are not gifted with imagi- nations so vivid, wild, and chaotic as himself and friends. the loss is ours and he can perhaps point out his own gain. Now in all honesty, and I may confess, simplicity,l make one grand, solemn, and sober charge against the Spiritualists and that is, that they are playing the deuce with our beautiful English langnesee ; not one word uted by them carries with it the ordinary English meaning. What are we to do, or what say, so that we shall under- stand one another ? If my friend tells me that the indi- vidual perfection, the grandest, and the highest life, yet attained by the individual man, is the result of ages of evo- lutionary growth, that the spiritnalised gout, or mind o: man, does not perish, but reappears as the leaven that eter- nally makes for righteourness and to helps to make to-day better than yesterday, well we wlI give it the serious at- tention the statement deserve But wh; nwe are told that the whole of what we hear, see, feel, smell, or touch, is not real, but only the result of imegiea..ion, that eve's, text quoted from Scripture carries with it a meaning entirely ' and completely new, so new in fact that our dictionaries become useless. Well, all I can say is that same old word "humbug." I remember some years ego attending a meeting of the Mormons in the Co-operative Hall, and one beastly old saint *ho could boast of his wives elicited fm the audi- ence repeatedly rounds of applause, and why? Simply because he was a perfect ma. ter in introducing iato bis lec- ture religious cent; his listeners failed to I. :e" lye that he was dosing them Mormonism pills, swear co ted with scrip- tural quotations. So it is with Spiritualiem. At the lecture I noticed persons cheering the lecturer, who, if toev bad understood what he was saying, would have receiled from him in pious ho, or. I give one instance, and Mr Edi;or, allow me to say I am not going in!ci any religious discus- sion; this is my last letter on Spiritualism. Christians generally are under the impressioe that Je is Christ an- peered, after tbe crucifixion, to Hie disciples—that is. made His physical existence, a subatantial certainty to them. This, according to Mr. Wallis, is not so; the imagination of the disciples is alone responsible for the whole thing. They alone clothed an immaterial and shadowless spirit, and called it Christ. "Blessed are the dead who die in the

Lord" is a meaningless phrase, because we do rot die. So one could go an all through scripture quoting t2lts for these Spiritualists to knock down, and C iristians eh: and encourage what is, aftar all, mere buffoonery. Can any sane man imagine a spirit beng at a loss to write inside a book slate without pencil, if the same spirit can introduce itself and bold upright a piece of pencil, four or five inches long, in a space where you could only manaia to place a sheet of piper? The thing is preposterous. The facts is the Spiritualists have thrown over the Christian God and the Christians' book, and have not courage to say so. CLIFFORD DIX.
