div.head: SHOCKING MURDER IN RAINHILL ASYLUM.
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER IN RAINHILL ASYLUM.

An affray between two inmates of the Rainhill County Asylum, involving the death of one of them, occurred on Wednesday afternoon, in the No. 5 refractory ward, which is situate in the western portion of the asylum. In the ward indicated there are about 25 patients of a suicidal, epileptic, or re- fractory character. Among the patients were Samuel Dalzell, 45 years of age, an ex-criminal, and another inmate named George Newton, a Roman Catholic priest, who came from Warrington. The men appear hitherto to have been on good teems in their lucid intervals, bUt it is stated that Dalzell be- came very violent on Wednesday afternoon, and in '.his frenzy he struck Mr. Newton on the foreheadl Ilwith a brush, killing him on the spot. It is also, I stated that Dalzell at times was the most violent patient in the ward. He entered the asylum as a patient in March last, having been removed from the convict prison at Woking, where he had just completed a sentence of ten years' penal servitude. which was passed upon him at the Liverpool Assizes in March, 1876, for wounding with intent to do grievous bod:ly harm. Dalzell was born in Liver- pool. He., is of fresh complexion, with black hair and hazel eyes, and is five feet seven inches in height. Mr. Newton had been an inmate of the asylum for about twelve years. He is described as being of a quiet disposition, though subject to ex- citable moments. Thomas Cowley is the "charge attendant" of the No. 5 ward. His assistant Is James Stanton, and there are two other attendants. The" charge attendant" was absent on Wednesday, and consequently Stanton was in charge. It is the practice for the patients in the No. 5 ward to keep the room clean and in order, and for this purpose sweeping brushes and hand shovels are provided. No inmate is al:owed to use a shovel unless under the supervision of an attendant, but the same pre- caution is not observed with regard to the use of the brushes. Dalzell is said on one occasion to have torn his wearing apparel to ribbons, and he was always the object of the especial care of the attendants. Particulars of the tragedy were imme- diately forwarded to the county coroner (Mr. Brig- house). _ . _

div.head: INQUEST AND VERDICT.
div.p: INQUEST AND VERDICT.

On Friday, Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at Rainhill Asylum, on the body of the Rev. George Newton, Roman Catholic priest, of Warrington, who for about twelve years had been an inmate in the asylum, but who was killed on Wednesday by being struck on the head with a brush by another lunatic, named Samuel Dalzell, who had undergone ten years' penal servitude, but who was brought to Rainhill in March last. Priso- ner was attended, by warders. Several relatives and friends of the deceased gentlemen were pre- sent; also two of Dalzell's btothers. Mr!. William Johnson was foreman ot the jury. The coroner and the jury proceeded to view -the body, after which the coroner, addressino. the jury, said the question of the sanity or insanity of the man who might possibly be charged with the death of this Newton was not a question for them. The only question for them was whether they thought Samuel Dalzell was the man who struck this George Newton or nqt, and whether be was criminally re- sponsible for the death, and if they thought so, then they would have to deal with this man Dalzell just as if he was sane, and send him for trial, The question of sanity or insanity would be dealt within another form.—The Coroner (to Dalzell, who had been brought into the room.)—The jury are about to inquire into the death of George Newton, and, of course, you will bear what is said, and you will have an opportunity of asking any questions if you like. —Dalzell made no answer.—Mr. Joseph Newton, the first witness called, said: I live at I, Carleton- street, Widnes. George Newton was my brother. Tie was a priest, and aged 45. I last saw him alive shortly after he came to the asylum—about ten years ago. I have seen his dead body to-day.--Evi- dence was then given as to the circumstances of , Newton's death, and witnesses deposed that he died immediately after having been struck on the head by Dalzell with a brush.—The jury returned a verdict of homicide against Dalzell, and he was com- mitted for trial on the capital charge.—Dalzell was subsequently removed to Kirkdale.
Qed

div.head: EX &MINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 11, 1886.
div.p: THE EX &MINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 11, 1886.
NEWS.
LATEST

The Duke of Westminster has remitted 25 per cent. of the rents now due from the tenants on his extensive es- tate in Flintshire. It is officially announced that the Queen has appointed H.R.H. the Duke of Connaught to be a member of the Council of the Government of the Bombay Presidency- . A Cabinet Council, at which all the Ministers except Lord Ashbourne and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach were pre- sent, was held at the Foreign Office on Friday. Russia, it is stated, has made concessions to Belgaria. The objection to the validity of the elections to the So- branje has been withdrawn. But there is a firm insistence on a change in the Regency. Tiln CLERICAL IMPOSTOR.—In Dublin, on Friday, Keatinge, the clerical impostor, was found guilty- of ob- taining money under false pretences, and was sentenced to eighteen months' bard labour. THE IMPERIAL INSTITTITE.—The Prince of Wales has despatched communications to Lord Lieutenants of counties, asking co-operation in bringing the subject of the Imperial Colonial and Indian Institute prominently before inhabi- tants of county districts. THREE MEN KILLED pi WALES.—On Thursday evening a shocking accident took place on the Cwmpennar incline, tear Moantein Ash. Seven men were proceeding to their work in empty trucks, and whilst they were going up the incline two loaded trucks dashed upon them. Michael Dris- coll, aged 17, was killed on the spot. A. man named David Davies had both his legs and arms broken, and died on the way borne. Daniel Cokelv. in addition to one of his legs being cut off, was badly injured about the head, and died at a late hour in the evening. Several other men were seriously injured. FHB COLIN CAMPBELL CasE.—On Thursday Mr. Justice Butt and.,a special jut y resumed the hearing of the Camp- bell divorce suits. The case fer Lord Colin havieg been concluded, the Attorney-General opened the case on behalf of the Duke of Marlborough, and Mr. Gully that for Captain Shaw. On Friday, Mr. Murphy opened the case for Col. But- ler, pointing out is sarcastic terms that the evidence against his client was confined to oke day only. Tho Solici- tor - General followed on behalf of Mr. Bird, and pointed out how flimsey was the evid- ence upon which Lord Colin relied to dishonour his wife and ruin his professional adviser. Lady Colin then gave evidence. She took great interest in chari- table undertakings in London, and is 1832 and 1883 sang at as many as forty charitable concerts. Four or five days after the consummation of the marriage she felt ill. Her husband knew she came to London from Leigh Court to sing at concerts. Her ladyship categorically denied all , charges brought against her.

div.head: SOUTHPORT LIFEBOAT CAPSIZED. THIRTEEN LIVES LOST.
div.p: THE SOUTHPORT LIFEBOAT CAPSIZED. THIRTEEN LIVES LOST.

The most appalling catastrophe that ham darkened the annals of Southport and neighbourhood since the calamity in 1869, when seven fishermen, were lost in a fog, occurred about one o'clock on• Friday morning, when the Southport lifeboat was cap- sized by the violence of the gale and thirteen men were drowned. It would appear that on Thursday a barque, of about 1,000 tons, was seen riding at anchor to the left of Southport. A terrific hurri- cane was blowing from the north-west, and much anxiety was felt for the safety of the vessel. About nine o'clock at night, several rockets were seen to rise in the direction where the vessel was last seen, and it being surmised that she was in trouble, the crew of the lifeboat Eliza Fernley were immedi- ately sumnapned. At twenty minutes to ten the boat was placed on the truck, to which were at- taeted several horses, and the crew proceeded along the shore in the direction of Ainsdale. On passing the Palace Hotel the distressed barque could be dis- tinctly observed, she having broken both cables, lost two masts, and got stranded on the main beach about half a mile on the north side of the Nereus,which was wrecked about two years ago. The lifeboat was launched successfully, and the crew of 16 hands all told Pulled gallantly towards the barque, which had continued to discharge rockets and show other signals of distress from the time she was first seen. After battling with the huge waves for over an hour, the crew got wiibin about 20 yards of the barque, and were gradually making headway when, coming broadside to the wind, the lifeboat was im- mediately capsized, and the whole of the crew were thrown into the water. Instead of righting herself, as she was supposed to do, the boat remained bottom upwards, the maiority of the crew being underneath her. Three of the crew, by great exer- tion, seized and retained their hold of the boat, and were saved. The bodies of ten other men were afterwards washed ashore. The whole of the bodies were removed to the Palace Hotel, Eirkdale. The disaster has cast the deepest gloom over the town, and the greatest sympathy is felt for the widows and families of the unfortunate men. Additional details show that five of the dea3ecl men remained under the lifeboat after it capsized for an hour in conversation, tney being only knee in water. Jackson escaped from underneath when the boat lifted a little, but Ball, in attempting to do the same thing, was severely hurt. The ()tiler three were either soffocated or drowned, and their bodies were found under the boat when it was Varned over. ANOTHER LIFE BOAT DISASTER. LOSS OF THE ST. ANNE'S BOAT AND EIGHT

The St. Anne's Life Boat put out to the wreck of the -.11.1e-r:ico from which the Lyi,ham boat rescued the crew of twelve on Taursday night, and has not since been seen.

SOUTHPORT, FRIDAY, 245 p.m. There have just been brought into the Birkdale (Southport) Palace stable yard five more bodies, making eight recovered of the crew of the St. Anne's lifeboat, three having previously been found on Birlabile Sands. Four of the men were found entangled in the ropes and yards. They were found under the boat about two miles and a half from Southport and cpposite ..kinsdale by a young man named Vincent Johnson. Another body was picked up about fifty-five yards from them, and the fifth in a pool close by. In the pockets of one was found a watch, the fingers of which had stopped at twenty minutes past two. The two life- boats had been found bottom upwipds between the Nereus, Which was wrecked about two years rgo, and the Mexico, of Hamburg, the crew of which they were t-ying, to save. it may be stated that the watch of Henry Hodge, a volunteer of the South- poit lifeboat crew, had stopped at five minutes past one. The number of bores now recover -1 is 21.

div.head: fCLIFFE CHOIR CONCERT.
div.p: fCLIFFE CHOIR CONCERT.

On Tuesday evening a concert of more than or- dinary merit and interest was given in Wycliffe Hall, by the choir of Wycliffe Congregational Church, assisted by well-known local vocalists and instrumentalists. The whole were under the con- ductorship of Mr. R. H. Pearson. There was a fairly good attendance. The humorous cantata depicting the incidents of John Gilpin's famous ride com- prised the first and principal part of the pro- gramme, and ',ll itself constituted a real musical treat. The solo vocalists were Miss Mary Walling- ton, Miss Unswor:Th, Dr. G. V. Mapei, and Mr. W. 11. Wallington. Mrs. R. H. Pearson had been expected to take part, but was, throwfh illness, unable to be present, and her place was filled by Miss Unsworth. The orchestra included the following ;—First vio- lins, Messrs. P. Caldwell and John Robe', '6s ; 2ad violin, Mr. T. Bancroft; viola, Mr. Littlewood; vio- loncello, Mr. If. Bond; bass, Mr. H. Whitfield; flutes, Messrs. Allan and W. F. Pearson; clarionet, Mr. F. Pendlebury; cornets, Messrs. W. Waterfield and W. Slater; piano, Mr. T. R. Ford; harmonium, Mr. J. B. Caldwell. The opening oveitu-e was ren- dered in a manner that made it assured that the performers were at home with the music. The choir, which numbered between thirty and forty voices, then commenced the deseiiption of the adventure of the famous linen draper by giv- ing the chorus "John Gilpin was a citizen." Miss Wallington, who undertook the important part of John Gilpin's spouse, did, it is almost needless to say, full justice to it, and her effortswerefrequenily applauded. She ,sang with her usual taste and skill. In the air "To-morrow is our wedding day "she was heard to particular advantage. Mr. Wallington sustained the part of Gilpin, and let his hearers know it right well in the air "I am a linen-draper bold," which he rendered with his usual clearness of vocalisation. Dr. Mapei, of Golborne, as the cal- endrer, was never at fault. In his opening recita- tive he made a good impression, and sustained it throughout. Miss tinsworth, who sang the con- tralto solos, deserves great credit, especially when it is considered that she undertook the part at a late moment. From a musical point of view her impersonation could not well have been better. The choruses were short, but they were crisp and catching, and as they were all well sung, they did credit alike to the performers and the conductor who so effectually wielded the baton. The orchestral accompaniment all through was excellent. The solos also, with one exception, were short. The exception was the bass solo, "Now see him mounted once again," which was capitally sung by Mr. W. H. Wallington, and which vividly describes the ride of the hero of the hour. The second part of the programme was commenced after a short interval with an orchestral rendering of , Boggeth's gavotte "Bewitching." Dr. Mapei sang '

NATIONALITIES BAZAAR AT RUNCORN. SPEECH BY MR. VERDIN, M.P. Bethesda Congregational schoolroom had a gay and feFtiv appearanceon Wednesday afternoon, when Mr. R. Verdin, M.P., opened "The Nationalities Bazaar, or the World's Fair." The object of the " fair " is fully explained in the speech of the pastor, the Rev. J. D. Thomas, whose remarks are reported below. Notwithstanding the stormy nature of the weather there was a capital attendance at the opening cere- mony. Amongst those present were the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the Rev. Thomas Cole (Garston), Dr. Mac- Lennan, Dr. McDougall, Captain Clark, Messrs. John Simpson, James Handley, J.P., I'. Handley, Beck, J. R. Frith, James Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, W. Handley, A. Cameron, W. Heatherington, A. Light- burn, Mr. and Mrs J. Littler, Mrs and the Misses Shaw, Mrs Brookes, Miss Norman, Miss Rigby, and the stallholders, &c. Mr. Robert Verdin, M.P., was accompanied by a party which included Mrs W. H. Verdin (Winsford), Miss Verdin, Mrs and Miss Cooke (Crewe), Miss Harrison (Birkenhead), Miss Perry, and Mrs%V. Handley. A hymn having been sung, The Rev. J. D. Thomas said the fair to which they in- vited their patronage and support was hoped to be a final effort in connection with a movement that was started nearly eight years ago. When be settled in Runcorn at the end of April, 1879, he found a sale of work in full swing, the end in view being the raising of funds with which to build a roam for the minister. The sum of £258 was rea- lised,and of that amount £135 was invested as a nucleus of a manse fund. From time to time, by means of cantatas, or oratories, and sewing meetings, that sum was considerably increased. In 1881 a subscription list was opened, and so generous was the response that they were fully justified in proceeding to purchase a plot of land and erect a house thereon. When he entered into possession of the manse in August of the following year, it was found that the total expenditure incurred was £714. They had only a little over £4OO in hand, so that it was necessary to raise a mort- gage of £303. It was intended ;3 endeavour to free them- selves from the debt when the jubilee of the opening of the chapel was celebrated last autumn, but the fates, in the shape of general elections, were against them. The ladies, with their usual pluck and heartiness, bad taken the matter up, and with a little gathered here, and a little gathered there, they had been able to get up the spectacle which now disclosed itself to their eves, by which they hoped to realise sufficient money not only to free the manse from debt, but also to enable them to do some very necessaay repairs to the chspel. In conclusion, Mr. Thomas expressed, on be- half of himself and the friends of the church, their deep sense of obligation to Mr. Verdin for his kindness in being present—(applause)—to open the bazaar. In the fact that they had coma from London specially to perform that duty they recognisEd the sincerity of Mr. Verctin's desire to serve them. (Applause.) Mr. Verdin, who WAS received with applause, expressed the pleasure he had in helping them in the good work they had undertaken, because, although not a resident in Ran- corn, he had been connected with it for too many years not to Lave an interest in the social and religious welfare of that important town. (Applause.) He was pleased to bear from their pastor that people from a great distance had contribu- ted various articles that had to be sold ; and well might they expect not only their own congreeatien and their neighbours te help them in their good work', but also oeople who held similar views throughout the county. (Hear, hear.) He trusted that at the close of the bazaar their ob- ject would be realised. He had always felt that tbe minister should live in a house belonging to the congrega- tion, and that that house should be free from debt. He be- lieved that if a minister must do his ditty in a Congrega- tional chapel money ought always to be provided for him, and he never °ROA to know that there was want in connec- tion with either his church or his schools. (Applause.) He was pleased to find that the officials of Bethesda Church were at this time of their history, the Jubilee year, making the attempt to clear the debt off the manse. They might really wonder why more had not been dune in the past, con- sidering that the church had existed for so many years, but although the Congregationalists had been in the town some 50 or 57 years, they had never been a rich or a large body; but he trasted the denomination would be larger than it had bean hitherto, even if it were not a rich one. (Hear, hear.) After a reference of the labours of the ladies in con- nection with that effort. Mr.Verdin declared the bazaat open amid loud applause Mr. James Handley, J.P.. proposed that a cordial vote of thanks be accorded to Mr. S erdiu for so readily consenting to open the bazaar, and for the manner in which he bad performed the ceremony. Mr. Verdin, when elected member for that division of Cheshire, said he put forward at all times for the well being of his constituents—(applause)-- and he Was glad that he was present that day engaged in that good work. It was not every member of Parliament tbat identified himself with the best interests—he meant the religious interests—of the people, but they had Mr. Verdin with them that day giving them excellent and wise counsel, and he shonld think that in future Mr. Thomas would be always treed from the cares of finance. He agreed with Mr. Verdin that a Congregational minister ought to be freed by his people from financial matters. He had enough to do to look after their higher, their spiritual, interests, and he hoped the esteemed pastor of that church would have plenty of money to carry on the useful work he was doing in the town. He felt a ‘deep debt of gratitude to Mr. Verdin for performing the ceremony that day, because his (Mr. Hand- ley's) family has, been connected with the church over since its foundation, 56 years ago. There were plenty of inanimate objects for sale; he did not know whether there were any animate objects for sale; but Mr. Verdin might do worse than have a Cheshire lass to minister to his wants during the six months in :he year he was attending to the nation's business in London. (Laughter.) He gave him that advice in return for what he had given them that after- noon. (Laughter.) Mr. John Simpson seconded the propesition with much pleasure. He mentioned the multifarious duties a member of Parliament was supposed and often did perform, and said he knew Mr. Verdin was always glad to lend a helping hand in connection with a good work. He hoped the funds of Bethesda Chapel would accomplish the object they had in view. He remembered the building of Bethesda Chapel, the jubilee of which they had recently celebrated, and he hoped that the good that had been done in the past was only an indication of the good to be done is the future. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas, it: putting the motion, announced that Mr. Robert Shaw had sent a bank note for £5. (Applause.) A gentleman from Southport (Mr. F. Fairhurst), who WAS A hearty worker in connection with the church for many years, had handed him a cheque for £lO. (Applause.) Mr. W. Handley remarked that Mr. Verdin had just whis- pered into his ear that he should be glad to give £2O to the bazaar. (Loud applause.) The motion was carried with enthusiasm, and Mr. Ver- din having suitably responded, the ladle.; commenced the sale of their wares. The room was gaily decorated with flags and bannerettes of various hues and devices, and the stalls were arranged in a unique and pleasing fashion ; the entire effect calling forth warm admiration. Each stall was representative of the architecture of a foreign clime, and according to the "guide book," the visitors were "transported in the same day from Runcorn to Zurich, from Zurich to Yokohama and Pekin, thence to the backwoods of Indiana, and finally to Alexandria of ancient fame." The Old Log Cabin, a correct imitation of the birthplace of President James A. Garfield, decorated with the national shield and flags of America, was presided over by Misses Chadwick, Millie Chadwick, Lydi- ate, Bessie Speakman, Coaf, Ainsworth, E. Littler, and Mrs Walton. In the Swiss Chalet the fair saleswomen were Mrs T. Handley. Mrs Beck, Misses Littler, F. Littler, and M. Beck : whilst in the Chinese Reception Hall, the guests were welcomed by Mrs Cameron, Mrs Williams, Misses Handley, F, Handley, and C. Handley. The occupants of the Old English Homestead (a model of the dwelling-place of Edward Underhill who attempted to assassinate Queen Mary) were Mrs Heatherington, Mrs Lacey, Mrs Powell, Mrs Hughes, Mrs N. Bracevirdle, and Miss Riley. The presiding-deities of the Egyptian Temple were Mrs Thomas, Misses Andrews, E. Riley, E. Ainsworth, Rhodes, and Ringland. The good things of the ^efreshment stall, arranged as a Japanese Tea Room, were dispensed by Mrs Chadwick, Mrs Reed, Mrs Hedley, Misses N. Handley, M. Littler, and E. Littler. All the stalls were laden with a profusion of beautiful articles of various descriptions, prin- cipally the work of tbe ladies of the congregation and their friends.. For the amusement of the visitors various enter- tainments were provided, and proved highly successful. The proceeds of the first day, including donatians amounted to £176. Of this sum £lO9 was taken at the stalls. SECOND DAY.

The second day's proceedings commenced at two o'clock • on Thursday afternoon, when a fair number of persons as- sembled, considering the stormy weather. Amongst those present were the Revs G Wood (Wesleyan) and J D Thomas; Mr and Mrs 0 Speakman, Miss Speakman, Mrs Wood, Mrs Brookes, Mrs Littler, Messrs John Simpson, F Fairhurst, James Handley, J.P., W Handley, T Handley, A Cameron, &c. Mr Speakman, in declaring the bazaar open, thanked the good friends at Bethesda Chapel for giving him that oppor- • tunity o: appearing amongst them. In times past he had . spent many happy moments there. He wa's spiritually born at Bethesda, and he thanked God that he was there that day to help them to clear the debt off the manse. He trusted that the bazaar would be successful, so that they would ant have to think about the debt, but only what, in his opinion, all churches should have to look after—the spiri- tual welfare of the flock and themselves. Mr. Speakman referred to the building of the school, and to the benefit to be derived from bazaars from a social point of view, and concluded with wishing the church and congregation of Bethesda success. (Applause.) Mr. Thoma's announced that Mr. Speakman had handed him a cheque for £lO. (Applause.) Mr. F. Fairhurst, of Southport, delivered a chatty and pleasant speech in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Speak- man for opening the bazaar. Mr. W. Handley seconded the motion with great pleasure. He mentioned the connection of the family of which Mr. Speakman was a member with Bethesda Chapel, and said Mr. tf peakman had ever shown A warm interest in the work of the chapel. He frequently attended their special gather- ings, and showed that he could not forget old Bethesda, and that day he had added very substantial evidence of the in- terest that he felt. (Applause.) The motion was carried with acclamation, and Mr. Speak- man suitably replied. The receipts on the second day amounted to £lOl as 31.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

LFROm OWN GWN CORREStONDENT.I 23, Old Broad-street, B.C. The course of the Stock Markets during the week might almost be traced on a weather chart, as applicable to both. Stirling at the opening of the week with a buoyancy un- equalled during the past month or two, prices continued to imprave until Wednesday, when a sudden fall, as unex- peed and es rapid as the barometer, set in. Foreign stocks, American securities, and Home investments all fel', and at one time to such an extent in some stocks as to be little short of a panic. Foreign stocks led the way owing to Berlin advices, where the failure to support Russian stocks led other markets to follow suit, and it is entirely due to the support in Berlin that Russians have continued for so long at such a firm rate. American rails especially fell, varying from one te three, and English rails responded, although to a less ex- tent, and in some instances, ia spite of increased traffic returns. The sensitive state of the market could not be more pointedly exemplified, the fall coming at a time when the tendency was all the other way, and the opti nistic feeling predominated. There has been a slight improvement since, and with reference to American rails nearly the only exception to the general fall was the Louis- ville, which actually rose t. Amongst Eoelisla rails Brigh- ton A's andNorthßritish were tbeonly lines that did not suffer much effect from the scare, the former having now nearly reached the best price it attained before the sudden fall al- luded to in my la3t, which was caused by unexpected heavy selling; the continued improvement in the traffic returas are saticient reasons for tke upward movement which has Characterised this stock. Among many curious enterprises recently brought before the investing public few excel that'of the North British Fresh Fish Supply Company, Limited. Why North Biitain should have been chosen as the most favourable spot for such an enterprise it is difficult to understand, as it is more than doubtful whether the shrewd men of the north will subscribe anything to such a cempany, and the directors as a whole are not such as to inspire confidence in their knowltdge of the business they undertake to direct.

CHURCH TENET:BANOS SoCIRTY.—On. Monday even- ing a branch of the above society. was commenced at War- grave. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Whitley, Rector and Rural Dean, and addresses were delivered by the chairman, the Revs. J. Hirst (Diocesan secretary), and E. J. Hack (curate), and Mr. Nickisson. A number of parishioners joined the society at the close of the meeting. THE Varm...2 Wosics.—We announced in our last issue the probability of a reduction in the working hours of the men employed at the Viaduct works. Short time has now been resorted by the Company. CONL-MT.—On Monday evening a concert was given in the boys' school, Pepper-street, in aid of the funds ef the Church of England Temperance Society. There was:a very good attendance. The concert was opened by a selection by the Lymm C.E.T.S. brass bold. Mr. J. Dale's rendering of the " Midahipmite " received a well-deserved encore. The Lymm String Band, Miss Broadbent (Aitrincham), Dr. Wil- liamson and Mr. Mercer (Warrington), also contributed to- wards the evening's entertainment, the comic songs of the latter being both redemanded. The concert concluded with Offenbach's operetta, "The blind beggars." Messrs. H. Clare and W. Joynson gave a very good impersonation of the two beggars.

A LOCAL WILL CASE- CHANCERY PROCEEDINGS. Vice-Chancellor Bristoe hadi before him on Tues- day, at the Chancery Court of the County Palatine of Lancsster, at St. George's Hall, Liverpool, a case in wh'ch Caroline Evans, the danghter of the late John A.ndsell, solictor, St. Helens, was the plaintiff, and John Hammill and James Galloway, executors and trustees a her father's will, were the defendants. The plaintiff sought a declaration that at the time of his death her father was trustee for herself of £l,oc preference stock in the Prescot Gas Company, and asked for an order for the executors to transfer the stock into her name, and to pay to her all the divi- dends received by them since the death of her father. Mr. Retch and Mr. Arkle were for the plaintiff. Mr. Maberley and Mr. Hopkinson appeared for the defendants. Mr. Rotch stated that the late Mr. And. sell left a fortune of some £40,000 or £50,000. At At the time of the marriage of the plaintiff to a Mr. Evans her father invested £l.OOO for her benefit in AI per cent. bonds of the Corporation of St. Helens. 'this was done in Mr. Andsell's name, and the interest was paid to the plain- tiff till Oatober, 1830. The bond was then paid off, and the £l,OOO was invested in 5 per cent preference stock of the Preccot Gas Company. The interest was paid plaintiff, and in September the deceased transferred a proportion, to the I value of £8,040, including the as stock, to the trustees in I trust for four daughters. Therefore at the time of hie death the deaeased was rot owner of this stock, baying parted with it. The deceased's will was made in January, 1883, and after seilirra out bequests, it directed that the residue of the teal and perronal effects should be divided equally between his six children. In March of that year the testator execu- ted a tolled in which he left piantiff £3 000 as a legacy in- stead of a siath share of the residue. The testator died in November, 1885, and the executors declined to transfer the gas stock to the plaintiff unless by an order of the court. Therefore, the plaintiff came before the court to ask whether there was a valid declaration of trust with regard to the investment. Mabberley for the defendants, argued that the testator merely intended to make voluntary provision for his daughter during his lifetime. There was no gift or investment to the plaintiff at all.—His Honour held that the £l,OOO was

a gilt of the plaintiff in trust on her marriage.—Mr. Ma- berley then contended that the £l,OOO was intendei to be included in the £3,000 legacy in the will.—Mr. Rotch dis- patel this, and pointed out that the will was not made for ten years after the gift.—Mr. Maherley submitted that the £l,OOO was ^n advance to the plaintiff, for which she would be liable as to any property or share of the estate coming to her under the will. The money never went out of the possession of the testator until 1883, when he settled it in ether trustees for the benefit of otber daughters.—The Vice-Chaecellor said the testator could not part with what did not belong; to him, for ha had already given the £l,OOO to the plaintiff as a marrrage settlement.—r. Rotel said that if there had been a breach of trust committed by the deceased, the plaintlff could have recovered from his es- tate.—The Vice-Chancellor, in giving his decision, said there most be a declaration that the £l,OOO gal stock was the property of the pl“i tiff, and was held by the tes- tator as trustee for her, lie did not consider that the de- ceased intended the lee.acy to include the gift of the £l,OOO made twelve years before his death. Therefore, the £l,OOO must be paid, though he could not say that the executors were not perfectly justified in seeking the opinion of the court.—Mr. Retch asked for an order of ingeiry to ascertain what loss the plaintiff had sustained by the voluntary set- tlement of the money in th,, ham's of trustees for other daughtere, and an orders for the executors to pay the loss with all costs in the action—The order was granted.

Ash, chaplai Ailey Hall, Northwich, and formerly curate of cry Magdalen, Paddington, London. WIFE NEGLECT.—At the Borough Court, on onday, a man named Joseph Higginson was sent o prison for a month for neglecting to support his wile, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union. It was stated that prisoner was in a position, if he would work, to earn ..E2 a week. On Tuesday, Patrick Patten, a laboarer, was charged with n )glectinfr to maintain his wire and family, and was sent' to prison for seven days. ST. PAUL'S MUTUAL IMPEOVEMENT SOCIETY.—On Saturday evening, the weekly meeting of the above socie.y was held in the Girls School, Heath Side, the Rev. S. Wilkinson in the chair, when an inter- esting paper was read by Mr. Andrew Rath hone on "Free Trade v. Fair Trade." The following mem- bers took part in the discussion which followed, namely, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, the Rev. R. Wood Samuel, Mr. D. W. Finney, Mr. Harding, Mr. j. Gib- son, and. M-,... James Knowles. FIRE IN THE FAIR GROUND.—At about three o'clock on Wednesday morning two show vans con- taining a model of the Manchester Ship Canal, and a quantity of scenery, were destroyed by fire. Tl vans were in the Fair Ground, where the model had been on exhibition. The fire seems to have originated in an adjoining tent. The sparks from a fire in a grate in the tent ignited some straw and set tire to the structure. The flames extended to the vans. which were destroyed before as=istance could be ob- tained. They belonged to Edward Amies, of Cross- street, Manchester. THE WARRING-TON ITARRIERS.—The first hanul- cap of the season for members of the above club took place on Saturday, from the Sankey Chapel House. The course lay along Liverpool-road to Bold Bridge. There were 13 entries, and ten started. At the half distance Waterworth led, being followed by Bellian, Maddock, Eden, and Chrimes. Water worth still held his own in the return journey, and .. eventually won easily. Result : `l, J Waterw orth ; 29 H. Maddock; 3, H. Sherlock; 4, G. Ratcliffe. T. Gl-leave, D. Walsh, T. Eden, J. Chrimes, G. Stokes, and J. Bellian also ran. The handicappers were Messrs. E. Burrows, J. Handles, and J. Dumbell. and Mr. E. Burrows officiated as starter, &c. The winner will receive a gold medal from the club. WORKMEN'S CLUB. On Tuesday evening the monthly meeting of the committee of this club was held, Mr. Potter (vice-president) in the chair. There was a full attendance of members, including ',l;.feBsrs. T. Hollingworth, I. Leeson, W. E. Stout, T. -R. Ash- croft, J. Bailey, A. Daniels, W. Ford, J. Godfrey, T. Heywood, W. Russell, T. Sanson, W. Sanson, T. Tickle, and R. E. Ellis. It was resolved, on the mo- tion of Mr. Ashcroft, seconded by Mr. P. Sanson, to send a letter of condolence to Mrs Maok,ie on the illness of the Mayor. It was decided, atter some conversation, that the resolution for openin- g the club as a free institution, as spoken of by the Mayor at the recent annual dinner of the committee, stand over until his worship could be present. A vote of thanks to Mr. Potter brought the proceedings to a close. _

TEMPERANCE MEETING AT ST. pAves•—on Mon- day evening a meeting was held in the school-room in connection with the Church of England Temper- ance Society. The Rev. S. Wilkinson presided, and in the course of an address alluded to the evils of intemperance, and the duty of all to do something towards counteracting them, Ile rem Pared the small sum spent upon church building With the enormous amount spent upon drink, lie Was very glad to welcome to Warrington another kind friend and warm temperance advocate in %lr. Langbam, who had kindly promised to speak during the even- ing. The following resolution was proposed by the Rev. J. J. Longhorn, principal of the Clergy Daugh- ters' S-hool :—" That this meeting recognises the wide-spread sin of intemperance to he the fruitful source of poverty,. crime, irreligion, and believes that such an association as the Church of England Temperance Society will be a likely means, in God's hands, of helping to reclaim the drini,karcl, of dis- couraging drunkenness, and of promoting the cause of temperance generally, amongst old and young." The resolution was seconded by the Rev. R. Wood Samuel, and carried unanimously. An entertain- ment was also given by the following ladies and gentlemen, naniely—Miss Wilkinson, Miss Chorlev, Mrs. Langharn, the Misses Pollitt, the Revs. S. W;1- kinson„T. J. Langham, and It. Wood Samuel, and Mr. J, Chorley.

The Public of Warrington are respectfully informed that the above Premises will shortly be opened for the SALE OF BUTCHERS' MEAT, MILK, BUTTER. GREENGROCERY. and FARM PRODUCE of every description at the Lowest Retail Prices. All the Articles sold will be the very beet of their respective kinds. -- THE BUTCHERING DEPARTMENT Will be open on Wednesday, 22nd December. 1888. Only Beasts and Sheep that are English Fed will be sold at the Stores, and the prices all round will be found to be exceedingly moderate. The blaughter House, in Orford-street, ie complete in all its details, and especial care will be paid to Cleanliness and Sanitary requirements. THE DAIRY, Which will open on Monday, January 10th, is being Atted up by the AYLESBURY DAIkcY CO. with all the latest appliances. All milk will be carefully tested at the Stores. sad RO milk will be sold that is not above standard. The retail price of milk during the winter months will be 3d. per quart, but persons pur- chasing books of tickets in advance have an allowance • made equal to about 10 per cent., thug reducing the price to about 21d per quart. Skim Milk. Butter, Fresh Eggs, and Cheese will also be sold in this de- partment. Milk will be delivered within a mile of the Stores twice daily. except Sunday,4 when it will be delivered in the Morning only. Orders for Milk supplies should be sent in, ad- dressed to the Manager of Farmers' Stores, Bewsey- estreet. Warrington, as soon as possible. The price of Books of Tickets is 10s: each, nett, each Book con- taining 88 Pint Tickets. THE GREENGROCERY DEPARTMENT will open on Weinesday, Nth. A fresh sup- ply of vegetables, Ac., will constantly be kept on hand. GENERAL PRODUCE. Samples of all kinds of Farmers' Produce including Cheese, Potatoes, Grain, Hay, At., will be kept at the Stores, and customers supplied on the shorted notice, THE EXCHANGE, for the free use of Farmers, and Corn and other Mer- chants geuerally, and CLUB ROOMS for the use of Members, will be formally opened in February. As all articles sold at the Stores will be disposed of at the LOWEST RETAIL PRICES, they must in every case be PAID FOR AT THE TIME OF PURCHASE, except the purchaser has a deposit account. Milk not purchased on the Ticket System as above, will be charged the FULL RETAIL PRICE, and must be paid for on delivery. The Directors are prepared to receive on DEPOSIT In prepayment of purchases to be afterwards made, sums of not less than £lO and not exceeding £5O, and to allow thereon an immediate discount of 2i per cent.
